Who  was  Elizabeth,  daughter  and  heiress  of  Powell  of  Wales,  and  wife  of  William  Forth  of 
Hadleigh  1  A  prolonged  and  most  careful  search  amongst  the  wills  at  Somerset  House  and  other 
Probate  Courts;  the  Fines,  Inquisitions,  Close  Rolls,  Patent  Rolls,  Ac.,  Ac.,  at  the  Record  Office;  and 
the  Pedigrees  and  Genealogical  Collections  at  the  Heralds’  College  and  elsewhere,  has  failed  to  elicit  a 
single  fact  in  answer  to  this  question.  As  Elizabeth  Powell  she  witnessed  the  will  of  her  future  hus¬ 
band’s  father  in  1510.  As  Elizabeth  Forth  she  became  the  mother  of  an  heir  in  1541.  We  should 
have  been  altogether  without  clue  to  her  identity  had  not  three  of  her  sons,  or  their  immediate 
descendants,  assumed  the  very  remarkable  quarterings  of  Powell  of  Whitchurch  in  Glamorganshire. 
The  eldest,  Robert  Forth,  caused  them  to  be  worked  into  the  great  gateway  of  Butley  Abbey,  where 
Davy,  the  Suffolk  Antiquary,  saw  and  noted  them  in  1810.  They  embellish  the  brass  of  William 
Forth,  the  third  son,  who  died  at  Hadleigh  in  1599.  And  John  Forth,  the  youngest  son,  seems  to 
have  assisted,  in  1611,  a  year  or  two  before  his  death,  in  the  preparation  of  the  “Emblazoned 
Pedigree  ”  of  Forth  and  Winthrop,  in  which  the  quarterings  of  Powell,  Brokenspeare,  Gwaringde,  Morley 
and  Vaughan  are  marshalled  in  all  their  splendour.  These  quarterings  were  allowed  to  Philip 
Forth,  her  grandson,  at  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1612.  This  being  the  case,  we  give  pedigrees  of 
the  one  and  only  family  of  Powell  to  whom  such  quarterings  could  possibly  have  belonged  :  and,  as 
Welsh  evidences  are  scarce,  excerpts  of  two  documents  which  help  to  establish  the  date  of  the  Appowell 
who  married  the  heiress  of  Vaughan  of  Methvr — the  conjectural  grandfather  of  Elizabeth  Forth.

The  Bourne  Pedigree  in  the  Visitations  of  Somersetshire,  1565 — 1623,  Ilarl.  MS.  1445,  describes  Sir  John  as  one 
of  the  principal  Secretaries  of  State  to  Queen  Mary.  In  his  will,  P.C.C.  29  Pyekeryng,  dated  18  May  1563,  he  leaves 
two  parts  of  his  Manor  of  Batenhall,  co.  Worcester,  to  Dorothy  his  wife,  and  the  residue  to  Anthony  his  son  and 
heir.  He  also  makes  provision  for  the  tuition  and  government  of  his  children  during  their  minority.  This  will  was 
proved  1  July  1575,  by  Dame  Dorothy  his  relict,  and  later  on  Administration  was  granted  to  Anthony  Bourne  the 
son,  21  July  1576,  his  mother  having  died.  From  the  letters  of  this  Anthony,  Add.  MS.  23,  212,  circa  1577,  we 
learn  that  he  and  Thomas  Powell  had  been  friends  together  at  Oxford,  he  having  on  one  occasion  rescued  the  latter 
from  the  police,  and  on  another  entrusted  him  with  money  for  the  payment  of  his  debts. 

The  earlier  ancestry  of  Powell  of  Whitchurch  is  given  us,  with  more  or  less  exactness,  in  the  pedigree  drawn  up 
by  the  order  of  King  Edward  the  Fourth,  when  he  created  William  Herbert  Earl  of  Pembroke  in  1460.  (See  Coxe’s 
“Tour  in  Monmouthshire,”  pp,  141,  421,  and  the  articles  on  the  Herberts  in  BurkeV  “ Extinct  Peerages.”)  For  further 
information  respecting  the  Whitchurch  family  the  reader  is  referred  to  the  “  Genealogies  of  Morgan  and  Glamorgan,”  by 
George  Thomas  Clark,  pp.  264,  265,  and  to  the  Wakeman  MS.,  an  admirable  compilation,  now  or  lately'  in  the  custody 
of  the  Society  of  Antiquaries.

Clopton  of  jWelforP. 


^rnt0rtal  Searings. 

The  Arms  of  Clopton,  Sable  a  bend  argent  between  two  cotices  dancettee  Or,  appear  upon 
the  seals  attached  to  their  deeds  and  charters  from  the  middle  of  the  fourteenth  century  downwards. 
Heading  the  Clopton  pedigrees  in  Harl.  MS.  1103,  a  contemporary  copy  of  the  original  Visitation 
of  Suffolk  by  William  Harvey,  Clarencieux  King  of  Arms  in  1561,  are  the  following  shields: — 

Clopton  of  Kentwell  Hall  in  Long  Melford. — Quarterly  of  six.  1.  Clopton;  as  above. 
2,  Mylde :  Argent,  a  lion  rampant  Sable,  over  all  a  fess  counter-compony  or  and  azure.  3,  Francis  : 
Gules,  a  saltire  between  four  crosses  patee  or.  4,  Iioydon ;  Chequy  argent  and  gules  a  cross  azure. 
5,  Knevitt :  Argent,  a  bend  within  a  bordure  engrailed  sable.  6,  Argent,  three  lions  rampant  gules. 
This  quartering  which  is  assigned  to  Kyrkham  in  Harl.  MS.  1560,  and  to  Belhouse  by  Dr.  Howard,  is 
common  to  both  families.  The  Crest  is  a  wolfs  head,  per  pale  or  and  azure,  and  the  Motto, 
“  Dor  en  avant.” 

Clopton  of  Liston. — Quarterly  of  four.  1,  Clopton.  2.  Mylde.  3,  Francis.  4,  Saye  ;  Per  pale, 
azure  and  gules,  three  chevrons  argent  voided  and  counter-changed  of  the  field,  over  all  a  crescent 
on  a  mullet  for  difference. 

Clopton  of  Sudbury. — Quarterly  of  six,  as  in  Clopton  of  Kentwell,  impaling  Peacock,  Gules,  on 
a  fess  argent,  between  three  plates,  each  charged  with  a  peacock’s  head  erased  azure,  as  many  mascles 
sable  ;  over  all  a  mullet  for  difference. 

Harl.  MS.  1820,  has  Clopton  of  Kentwell,  Quarterly  of  six,  as  before,  impaling  Baruardiston  ; 
Azure,  a  fess  dancettee  ermine,  between  six  cross  crosslets  argent. 

Harl.  MS.  1560,  fo.  5,  has  Quarterly  of  eleven.  1,  Clopton.  2,  Mylde.  3,  Francis. 
4,  Knevett.  5,  Kirkham.  6,  Bozun  of  Lincolnshire ;  Argent,  three  bird-bolts  gules.  7,  Uffleete ; 
Argent,  on  a  fess  azure  three  fleurs  de  lis  or.  8,  Deane ;  Sable,  two  bars  argent  within  a  bordure 
gules.  9,  Paynell  ;  Gules,  two  chevrons,  within  a  bordure  argent.  10,  Argent,  semee  of  fleurs  de 
lis,  a  lion  rampant  sable.  11,  Sable,  three  cinquefoils,  all  within  a  bordure  argent.  The  whole 
being,  apparently,  the  achievement  of  Mary  Clopton,  afterwards  the  wife  of  Sir  William  Cordell. 

The  Shield  of  Clopton,  quarterly  of  twenty,  from  Sir  William  Clopton’s  monument  in  Melford 
Church,  is  pictured  and  described  in  Dr.  Howard’s  edition  of  Harvey’s  Visitation  of  Suffolk. 


CLOPTON  OF  MELFORD. 


137 


The  wolf’s  head,  as  Clopton’s  Crest,  appears  on  the  seal  attached  to  a  charter  of  Sir  William 
Clopton  of  the  third  year  of  Henry  the  fourth,  1402.  It  is  occasionally  represented,  as  on  the 
Clopton  monument  at  Lyston,  issuing  from  a  ducal  coronet. 

A  great  number  of  Clopton  wills,  deeds,  pedigrees,  &c.,  have  been  printed  in  Dr.  Howard’s 
edition  of  “  Harvey’s  Visitation  of  Suffolk,”  vol.  i,  pp.  20 — 136.  Some  additional  evidences 
from  the  De  Banco  Rolls  and  other  sources  are  given  below.

Sir  Simon  D’Ewes,  who  married  the  heiress  of  the  Cloptous  of  Kentwell,  made  elaborate 
collections  relating  to  their  history,  which  will  be  found  amongst  the  Harleian  Charters  and  MSS. 
in  the  British  Museum.  He  deals  much  with  the  same  family  in  his  “Autobiography,”  a 
Bowdlerised  edition  of  which  was  printed  in  two  volumes  in  1845.

5Htll  nf  William  Clapton,  1612. 

October  25th  1612.  Mr  William  Clapton  Esquyre  did  in  our  hearing  will  &  bequeath  all  his 
moveable  goods  &  chattels  what  soever  vnto  his  sonne  William  Clapton  ;  &  being  demaunded  yf  his 
meaning  were  not  that  his  other  sonne  Mr  ffrancis  Clapton  &  Mr  Whitcroft  should  not  have  any 
of  them  he  answeared  that  he  would  leave  that  to  his  sonh  William  his  discretion ;  &  this  he 
iustifyed  to  be  his  will. 

P  me  dohanem  ffirmin  eleriem. 

Thomas  Neavell. 

ExtlG  14  Januarij  1612. 

Comiss.  London,  Essex  and  Herts.,  1612. 

Obviously  the  will  of  William  Clopton  of  Liston,  who  died  on  the  25th  of  October,  1612, 
leaving  William  Clopton,  his  son  and  heir,  Francis  Clopton,  his  second  son,  and  a  daughter,  Mary, 
married  to  George  Whetcroft  of  Eye  in  Suffolk. 


Will  of  (ffilliam  Clopton,  1640, 

This  is  the  last  will  and  testament  of  mee  William  Clopton  thelder  of  Groton  in  the  county 
-of  Suff  gent  made  and  published  this  first  day  of  November  1640  I  commend  my  soule  into  the 
hands  of  Allmighty  God  stedfastly  believeinge  throughe  the  onelie  meritts  and  passion  of  my  blessed 
saviour  Christ  Jesus  to  obtain  pardon  of  all  my  sinns.  I  giue  vnto  my  loving  wife  my  customary 
lands  in  Groton  holden  of  William  Hobart  Esquire  as  of  his  mannor  of  Lynsey,  of  John  Sampson 
Esquire  as  of  his  mannor  of  Lillesey  cum  Sampsons  Hall  in  Carsey,  and  of  Isaack  Appleton  Esquire 
vnto  the  full  tearme  of  eightene  yeares.  And  after  the  expiracoii  of  the  said  tearme  I  will  that 
all  said  customary  lands  shall  come  to  my  sonne  William  and  his  heires  for  ever  Ry  Indenture 
of  demise  bearinge  date  the  seaven  and  twentieth  of  October  last,  I  the  said  Wm  Clopton  and  the 
said  William  Clopton  my  sonn,  have  letten  vnto  John  Sampson  the  younger  gent  and  Robert 
Sampson  gent  all  those  my  mannors  of  Chastlynes  Chipley  and  Sandefords  and  all  other  my  freehold 
lands  in  the  county  of  Suff.  vnto  the  full  tearme  of  eighteene  yeares,  which  lease  was  made  in 
trust  for  the  raiseing  of  porcons  for  my  younger  sonnes  and  daughters.  My  meaneinge  is  that  said 
lessees  shall  assigne  vnto  my  said  wife  as  well  the  said  Indenture  of  demise  as  alsoe  the  said 
premisses,  and  that  my  wife  (the  yearelie  rent  of  fower  score  pownds  beinge  deducted)  shall  raise 
porcons  for  my  younger  children,  that  is  to  say  for  every  one  of  them  (except  my  youngest  sonne) 
twoe  hundred  pownds  a  piece  as  they  bee  in  senioiity  one  before  another.  And  whereas  I  am 
seized  of  one  coppiehold  tenement  lyeinge  in  Lynsey  holden  of  the  said  William  Hobart,  of  which 
mannor  the  custome  is  that  coppiehold  estates  doe  discend  to  the  youngest  sonne,  my  will  is  that 
my  executrix  shall  shall  pay  vnto  my  said  youngest  sonne  the  somme  of  eightscore  pownds  onely 
and  noe  more.  I  doe  heartily  desire  my  said  executrix  that  my  sonn  Walter  bee  contyuued  at  the

vniversity  of  Cambridge  vntill  one  yeare  after  hee  shall  heve  taken  the  degree  of  a  Master  of 
Arts,  And  I  doe  nominate  my  loving  wife  Alice  Clopton  to  bee  the  sole  executour.  Probatum 
vicesimo  Septimo  die  Novembris  1640  Juramento  Alicie  Clopton  relicte. 

P.C.C.  148  Coventry. 

It  was  Thomasine  Clopton,  the  sister  of  the  testator,  who  became  the  second  wife  of  John 
Winthrop  of  Groton,  afterwards  Governor  of  Massachusetts,  6  Dec.  1615.  Her  marriage  settlement 
is  given  at  page  22.  The  pathetic  story  of  her  death,  but  one  year  later,  as  penned  by  her  husband, 
will  be  found  in  Vol.  I,  pp.  79-89,  of  the  “  Life  and  Letters  of  John  Winthrop.” 


SStiil  at  |3okii  ffiiopton,  1730. 

I  Poley  Clopton  of  Bury  Sk  Edmonds,  Doctor  in  Physick,  resigning  my  soul  into  the  hands  of 
the  ffather  of  Mercys  do  publish  this  my  last  will.  Impris  I  give  and  devise  unto  James  Reynolds 
Esqr  Lord  Cheif  Baron  of  his  Majesty’s  Court  of  Exchequer,  Thomas  D’Gray,  Thomas  Barnardiston, 
Baptist  Lee  and  John  Moyle  Esquires,  John  Turnor  Esqr  the  present  Recorder  of  Bury,  my  brother  in 
law  Mr  Edward  Crispe,  Mr  William  Turnor  and  Mr  Henry  Turnor  his  son,  Mr  Walter  Raye,  Mr 
Samuel  Raye,  Mr  Edward  Isaack  Jackson  and  Mr  Joshua  Grigby  all  of  Bury  aforesaid  and  to  their 
heires  so  much  of  my  mannors  &c.  in  Suffolk  and  Essex  (other  than  my  seat  called  Lyston  Hall)  as 
they  shall  think  fit,  not  exceeding  the  yearly  value  of  three  hundred  pounds,  upon  trust  that  they 
shall  erect  a  convenient  house  in  Bury  for  the  reception  and  maintenance  of  twelve  poor  people, 
inhabitants  of  Bury,  viz*  six  men  and  six  women  of  the  age  of  sixty  yeares  and  upwards,  and  shall 
after  said  house  shall  be  built,  imploy  the  rents  in  the  maintenance  of  the  said  poore  people.  Also  I 
will  that  when  said  trustees  shall  be  reduced  to  five  that  those  surviving  shall  convey  the  premises 
to  eight  other  inhabitants  of  Bury  under  the  trust  hereinbefore  expressed  and  so  toties  quoties  for 
ever.  Item  I  give  to  my  cousin  Richard  Clopton  of  Coney  Weston  one  thousand  pounds  for  the 

better  support  of  himself  and  ffamily  :  to  my  cousin  Thomas  Clopton  the  sum  of  two  hundred 

pounds  and  to  my  cousin  Walter  Clopton  the  like  sum  :  to  my  kinswoman  Mrs  Elizabeth  Tyler 
the  like  sum  and  to  my  kinswoman  Mrs  Elizabeth  Murrills  two  hundred  pounds.  Item  to  the 

Master  and  ffellows  of  Queen’s  Colledge  in  Cambridge  twenty  pounds.  To  my  relation  Mr  James 

Sturgeon  a  guinea  to  buy  a  ring  in  remembrance  of  me.  To  the  poor  of  James  in  Bury  ffifty 
pounds  and  of  S1  Mary’s  parish  ffifty  pounds  to  be  distributed  amongst  such  of  the  poor  who  do 
not  take  Collection.  To  the  poor  of  Liston  in  Essex  ten  pounds.  I  desire  my  body  may  be 
interred  in  Lyston  chancell  and  a  decent  monument  affixed  in  the  wall  near  it  with  an  inscription 
to  be  written  by  the  Reverend  Mr  Needeu  of  Rougham  to  whom  I  -  give  two  guineas  for  his 
trouble — the  monument  not  to  be  expensive  nor  under  one  hundred  pounds  charge.  As  to  Lyston 

Hall  and  all  other  my  reall  estate  I  give  to  my  dear'y  beloved  sister  Elizabeth  the  wife  of 

Mr  Edward  Crispe  and  to  her  heires  for  ever.  All  the  residue  to  my  said  sister  to  be  at  her  own 

disposal.  I  appoint  (her)  sole  executrix  this  SO1,11  October  1730.  Probatum  23  Nov.  1730. 

P.C.C.  301  Auber.

This  Inquisition,  which  so  concisely  records  the  descent  of  Sir  William  Tyndal  from  Lord 
Scales,  is  one  of  the  four  which  detail  the  possessions  of  Anthony  Woodville,  Earl  Rivers,  in 
Norfolk,  Suffolk,  Hertfordshire  and  Cambridgeshire.  By  some  mediaeval  mistake  these  Escheats 
were  placed  with  those  of  the  first  year  of  Henry  VII.  Their  entry  in  the  Calendar,  “  Escaet. 

Hen.  VII,”  stands  thus  “  Antonij  nup  Comit  Ryvers  :  38  Norff.  :  Suff.  39  :  37  Hertf.  :  Cantebr.  36. 

These  offio  are  fyled  in  anno  primo  and  were  fownde  in  anno  scdo.”

Hatnsborougl). 


The  family  of  Rainsborougli  or  Rainborough,  often  spelled  Rainborow,  so  prominently  associated 
with  the  naval  service  of  the  Stuart  period  and  with  the  army  of  the  Commonwealth,  is  believed  to 
have  originated  in  Suffolk,  though  proof  is  wanting.  The  distinguished  naval  commander  William 
Rainsborough,  whose  successful  expedition  against  Salee  is  a  matter  of  history,  was  M.P.  for  the 
Suffolk  sea-port  of  Aldborough  in  1640,  and  his  father,  Thomas  Rainborow  of  East  Greenwich,  is. 
supposed  to  have  been  grandson  to  the  Thomas  Raynburghe  of  Ipswich,  who  made  his  will  in  1544. 
There  was  active  communication  between  these  two  ports  in  Tudor  days,  and  the  name,  an  unusual 
one,  disappeared  from  the  one  place  a  little  before  it  is  found  in  the  records  of  the  other.  For 
much  valuable  information  relative  to  this  family  and  the  correction  of  various  errors  which  had 
found  their  way  into  print,  see  the  “New  England  Genealogical  Register,”  Vol.  xl,  pp.  158 — 171.

Thomas  Cooke,  the  testator,  was  grandfather  of  Colonel  Thomas  Cooke,  M.P.  for  Essex  in 
1654,  whose  will  is  given  at  page  80.  According  to  the  pedigree  entered  in  the  Essex  Visitations 
( Harl .  MSS.  10SS,  1187  and  llf.32)  he  had  three  wives — Susan,  daughter  of  .  .  .  Brand  of 
Boxford  in  Suffolk,  the  mother  of  his  children ;  Elizabeth,  daughter  of  ,  .  .  North  of  Colchester ; 

and  Margaret,  daughter  of  .  .  .  Rice  of  Bures  St.  Mary  in  Suffolk.  Particulars  of  his  family 

and  descendants  will  be  found  in  the  Histories  of  Essex  by  Morant  and  Wright.

Thomas  Aleyn.  was  the  representative  of  the  Aleyns  of  Icklingham  in  Suffolk,  a  township 
which  they  acquired  through  the  marriage  of  their  ancestor,  John  Aleyn,  Baron  of  the  Exchequer, 
temp  King  Henry  VII.,  with  Constance,  daughter  and  heiress  of  William  Gedding.  The  will  is 
sealed  with  the  Aleyn  Arms,  per  bend  rompu  argent  and  sable,  six  martlets  counter-changed. 
Pedigrees  of  the  family  are  given  in  the  Visitations  of  Suffolk  (Harl.  MSS.  891  and  1560)  and  of 
Devonshire  (Harl.  MS.  1080).  Allen  quartered  Gedding,  Aspall,  Peache  and  Watvyle  (Barretts  MS.  fyc.)

ever.  Itm  Vnto  my  daughter  Ann  Clarke  widowe  two  hundred  pounds.  If  my  daughter  Ann

Read  <fc  Elizabeth  Clarke  to  each  of  them  a  gold  ring  of  twentie  shillings  price.  To  my  loving 
ffriend  William  Parsons  now  of  Birchanger  clarke  &  to  his  wife  &  daughter  Margarett  Parsons

The  above  is  founded  upon  the  Pedigree  of  Read,  with  numerous  wills,  &c.  given  in  the  “  Ancestry  of  Priscilla  Baker,”  by 
her  descendant  William  S.  Appleton  of  Boston,  U.S.  ;  the  Read  aud  Cooke  pedigrees  in  the  Harleian  MSS.  ;  and  the  very 
genealogical  Chancery  Proceedings  in  Veyscy  contra  Read ,  Reynardson,  I,  117.  in  the  Public  Record  Office.  Numerous  letters  from 
members  of  the  Reade  family  and  its  connections  are  to  be  found  in  the  six  volumes  of  selections  from  the  Winthrop  Papers 
published  by  the  Massachusetts  Historical  Society,  while  many  others  are  still  unpublished.

The  preceding  portion  of  this  work  has  been  devoted  to  the  Winthrops  of  Groton  and  the 
families  allied  to  them.  The  five  following  evidences  would  have  been  included  in  proper  order 
had  they  come  to  light  in  season,  and  they  are  now  appended  before  passing  to  wholly 
different  subjects. 


Mill  of  ffimge  Still,  1560. 

Ano  Dili  1560,  Jauar  30.  I  George  Styll,  bacheler  in  Divinitie  and  felowe  of  S1,  John’s 
colledge  in  Oambridg,  being  sicke  in  body  but  sownd  in  mynde,  make  this  my  last  wiil.  I  bequeath 
my  whole  self  to  my  great  and  good  god  in  whom  onlye  I  costantly  beleve.  My  worldly  goods 
I  bestowe  theim  wholie  on  Mr  John  Styll  Doctor  of  Divinitie,  desyering  hym,  yf  he  thincke  so 
good  to  gyve  to  my  father  my  gelding.  All  my  books  (yf  my  said  brother  thincke  good)  I  gyve 
to  my  nephew  John  Styll  my  said  brother  his  eldest  sonne.  To  my  syster  Mrs  Ann  Styll,  my 
said  brother’s  wieff,  I  gyve  my  twoe  carpetts,  Ac.  To  Joan  my  sister  a  featherbedd,  Ac.  To 
Elizabeth  my  sister  three  or  four  pounds.  I  bequeath  for  four  yeres  after  my  death  yearlie  xs 
to  be  distributed  vnto  the  poore  of  Whatfeld  in  Suffolk  on  Xpemas  daye.  To  the  three  wytnesses 

of  this  my  wyll,  Mr  James  Byll  bachelor  of  Divinitie,  Mr  Peter  Wythipoll  and  Authonye  Higgyn 

Mr  of  arte,  I  bequeath  to  eche  of  theim  a  flrenche  crowne  to  make  them  a  ringe  to  remebre 

me  wtball.  For  all  my  apparell  at  Hadley  and  elsewhere  1  gyve  it  wholie  to  my  said  brother 

John  Still.  I  request  of  him  as  my  last  peticon  that  he  nevr  lett  Sr  Gedney  want  so  long  as 
he  lyveth.  Adm  to  Jo.  Styll,  S.T.P.,  fratri  naturali  et  ltimo  Georgij  Styll,  S.T.B.,  vicesimo  septimo 
die  Junij  1585.  Wills,  University  of  Cambridge,  1558 — 1602,  fo.  95. 

For  the  will  of  the  testator’s  brother,  successively  Bector  of  Whatfield,  Vicar  of  Hadleigh 
and  Bishop  of  Bath  and  "Wells,  and  for  their  pedigree  see  pp.  74-76.  Alice  Still,  their  sister, 
became  the  first  wife  of  the  third  Adam  Wintlirop  in  1574,  and  died  s.p.  in  1579. 

A  fine  pedigree  of  the  Stills  of  Dorsetshire,  descendants  of  the  Bishop,  with  some  account 
of  the  family,  will  be  found  in  Hutchins’  History  of  that  County,  Vol.  III.

It  would  now  seem  that  Maryon  Burde  alias  Bryde  of  Ipswich  and  Richard  Byrde,  her 

husband,  were  identical  with  the  “  Richarde  Burde  of  Ipswich  and  my  sister  his  wief,”  who  are 

referred  to  in  the  will  cf  the  second  Adam  Winthrop  (See  page  13).  Prolonged  research  has  failed 
to  discover  any  other  Richard  Burde  of  that  place  and  period.  It  has  been  assumed  that  Richard 
Burde’s  wife  was  the  own  sister  of  Adam  Winthrop,  but  the  evidence  of  the  wills  of  John  Cely 

of  Bury  St,  Edmunds,  1557,  and  of  Alice  Cely,  his  widow,  1558,  discovered  since  the  issue  of 

the  earlier  pages  of  this  volume,  creates  a  presumption  that  she  was  really  the  step-sister  of  Alice 
Henny  or  Hunne,  Adam  Winthrop’s  first  wife,  who  died  young  in  1538.  Alice  Cely,  previously 

wife  of  -  Hunne,  died  in  1558,  leaving  three  Hunne  children  then  surviving  and  a  stepdaughter, 

Maryon  Cely,  wife  of  Richard  Byrde  alias  Bryde  of  Ipswich,  clearly  the  defendant  in  “Hunne 
contra  Burd.”  She  also  left  a  son,  William  Cely,  who  is  believed  to  be  the  William  Cely  who 
married  Adam  Winthrop’s  daughter,  Mary.  For  the  will  of  Richard  Byrde  and  further  particulars 
of  the  families  of  Hunne  and  Cely  see  hereafter,  pp.  221-223  (Goodwin  of  Bull’s  Hall).

porcoh  wch  she  maye  claime  by  the  custome  of  the  cittie  of  London  and  in  recompence  of  all

bestowed  vpon  my  ffunerall.  Vnto  the  poor  of  Battersey  three  pounds.  To  the  poore  prisoners 

in  the  two  Compters  and  in  Ludgate  sixe  poundes.  The  residue  of  my  goods  I  whollie  giue  to 
all  my  children,  parte  and  parte  like.  I  ordaine  my  trustie  and  welbeloved  brother  in  lawe, 
William  Cranmer  executor.  And  overseers  I  name  my  lovinge  freinde  Mr  Humfrye  Phippes  and 
my  lovinge  brother  in  lawe  Mr  Edwarde  Ditchfeilde.  Probatum  vicesimo  primo  Septembris  1619, 
juramento  WiBmi  Cranmer,  executoris.  P.C.C.  88  Parker. 

John  Whittingham  and  Joshua  Winthrop,  his  brother  in  law,  had  married  two  sisters, 
daughters  of  Vincent  Norrington,  Citizen  and  Grocer  of  London,  whose  nuncupative  will,  dated  on 
or  about  the  second  of  January  1597,  was  proved  on  the  nineteenth  of  the  same  month  by  Joan 
Norrington,  his  relict.  [P.C.C.  5  Lewin.]  “  Sicke  in  body  and  in  danger  of  death  he  did  giue 
all  that  euer  he  had  unto  Joane  his  loueing  wife,  sayinge  that  if  he  had  five  thousand  pounds 
more  he  wold  not  giue  anie  from  her.”  On  the  12th  of  November  1617,  a  commission  was 
issued  to  Sarah  Whittingham,  one  of  the  sisters  referred  to,  for  the  final  administration  of  her 
father’s  estate.  It  was  Mary,  the  other  sister,  who  married  Joshua  Winthrop,  sometime  of  London, 
and  after  of  Bandon  in  Ireland,  whose  kindred  and  connections  will  be  found  in  the  pedigree  of 
Winthrop  of  Groton,  at  page  27.

Mary  Paul  of  Norwich,  widow,  16th  March  1737.  My  moiety  of  my  reputed  manor  and 
capital  messuage  and  of  all  my  lands  in  Polstead,  Boxford  and  Assington  in  the  county  of  Suffolk, 
also  moiety  of  messuage  and  lands  in  Mendlesham  in  the  said  county,  unto  my  loving  sister  Sarah 
Fones.  After  her  decease  all  said  messuages  lands  woods  &c.  in  Mendlesham  unto  my  three  grand¬ 
children,  Ann  Paul,  Mary  Paul  and  Samuel  Paul,  the  son  and  daughters  of  my  son  in  law  John 
Paul  of  Mile  End  Green  in  the  county  of  Middlesex  mariner,  and  to  their  respective  heirs  as 
tenants  in  common.  And  from  the  decease  of  my  said  sister  Sarah  Fones  I  give  my  moiety  of 
said  Manor  in  Polstead  Ac.  to  Nehemiah  Lodge  of  the  city  of  Norwich,  gentleman,  forever,  in  trust 
to  sell  and  receive  rents  and  to  pay  legacies.  That  is  to  say,  to  my  cousin  Katherine,  the  wife  of 
Mr  John  Nuthall.  citizen  and  Alderman  of  Norwich  the  sum  of  fifty  pounds  :  to  my  cousin  Sarah 
their  daughter  one  hundred  pounds  :  to  my  cousin  John  Jackson  woollen  draper  fifty  pounds :  to 
my  cousins  Elizabeth  Smyth,  Abigail  Smyth,  and  James  Smith  of  Norwich  each  fifty  pounds  : 
to  my  cousin  Elizabeth  Baist  the  wife  Mr  Edward  Baist  ten  pounds  :  to  my  cousin  Sarah  Beamont 
the  wife  of  Mr  John  Beaumont  ten  pounds  :  to  my  cousin  Mary  Lodge  the  wife  of  said  Nehemiah 
Lodge  ten  pounds  :  to  my  cousin  Martha  Jackson  twenty  pounds  :  to  my  grandson  John  Paul 
fifty  pounds  and  to  Thomas  Paul  son  of  said  John  Paul  at  his  age  of  twenty  one  years.  To  poor 
ministers  or  ministers  widows  and  other  poor  persons  the  sum  of  twenty  five  pounds  out  of  my 
South  Sea  Annuities.  My  sister  Sarah  Fones  to  be  sole  executrix.  Proved  12  October  1738  by 
oath  of  Sarah  Fones,  spinster.  P.C.C.  240  Brodrepp. 

The  will  of  John  Paul  of  Bethnal  Green,  co.  Middlesex,  Gentleman,  the  husband  of  testatrix, 
was  proved  in  the  Prerogative  Court  in  1733  (P.C.C.  15  Ockham),  and  that  of  Sarah  Fones,  her 
sister,  in  1745  (P.C.C.  J)6  Edmunds).  For  pedigree  and  wills  of  Fones  of  Nusteed,  see  pp.  83-87.

The  Arms  of  Cullum  of  Hawstead  are  Azure,  a  chevron  ermine  between  three  pelicans  or,  vulr.iug  themselves  proper.  Crest — 
A  lion  sejant  or,  supporting  between  the  paws  a  column  argent,  the  capital  gold.  Motto — “  Sustineatur.” 

The  very  numerous  wills,  grants,  extracts  from  parish  registers,  &c.,  upon  which  the  above  pedigrees  are  founded,  have  appeared 
in  “Miscellanea  Genealogiea  et  Heraldica,”  Second  and  Third  Series,  and  are  being  privately  reprinted,  with  illustrations  and  addenda, 
by  Mr.  G.  Milner-Gibson  Cullum,  F.S.A.  Much  respecting  the  family  will  be  found  in  the  well-known  “  History  of  Hawstead,”  by  the 
Rev.  Sir  John  Cullum,  Bart.,  F.R.S.,  F.S.A.,  and  in  the  “History  of  Thingoe  Huudred,”  by  John  Rokewode  Gage.

close  Argent,  holding  in  the  beak  a  branch  of  laurel  proper  and  resting  the  dexter  claw  on  a  bridle  bit  Or.

J&oltoero  of 


Armorial  Hearings. 

At  the  Visitation  of  Suffolk  in  1612,  by  Raven,  Camden’s  deputy,  the  Arms  allowed  to 
“John  Boldero  of  Berry,  descended  from  William  Boldero  of  Fornham  Martin,”  were — “Per  pale,  or 
and  azure,  a  saltire  counterchanged,  with  a  crescent  for  difference.”  The  Crest  of  “  Bolderoe  per 
Cooke,  Cla:  6  of  September  1576,  18  of  Eliz.,”  as  tricked  by  Raven  in  his  note  book,  Harl. 

MS.  1820,  fo.  45b,  was  “  a  greyhound  current  gules,  collared  or.”  At  fo.  2,  is  a  drawing  of  the 

Arms  of  “  Boldero  and  his  wife  Tilliote,”  viz.,  Boldero,  with  the  crescent,  impaling  “  Argent,  a  lion 
rampant  gules,  over  all  a  bend  azure.”  The  original  shield,  without  the  crescent,  and  the  crest  of 
1576,  will  be  found  upon  Boldero  monuments  at  Ixworth,  and  on  the  brass  of  George  Boldero  in  St. 
Mary’s  Church,  Bury  St.  Edmunds.  They  are  still  used  by  his  descendants  ;  some  of  whom,  however, 

about  the  close  of  the  eighteenth  century,  changed  the  crest  to  a  greyhound  sejant.  The  escutcheon 

on  the  monument  to  Dr.  Edmund  Boldero,  in  Jesus  College  Chapel,  Cambridge,  who  was  the 
seventh  son  of  “John  Boldero  of  Berry,”  is  charged,  as  might  have  been  expected,  with  the 
crescent  allowed  to  his  father. 

Another  Coat  of  Arms  recorded  in  the  Heralds’  College,  but  not  in  the  Visitation  of  1612, 
was  granted  to  Francis  Boldero  of  Bury  St.  Edmunds,  who  died  in  1579,  “  Per  pale,  argent  and 
azure,  a  saltire  counterchanged;  on  a  chief  of  the  first  three  griffins’  heads  erased  of  the  last.” 
Harl.  MS.  1820,  gives  the  colours  of  this  Shield  as  or  and  azure,  together,  with  a  special  Crest, 
“  A  lion’s  gamb  erased  or,  grasping  a  saltire  azure.” 

Drawings  of  the  Arms  and  Crest  of  “John  Boldero,”  above-mentioned,  will  be  found  in 
Harl.  MS.  1449,  fo.  71b,  and  in  Add.  MS.  5524,  fo.  18b.

By  her  Inquisition  post  mortem,  4  and  5  P.  and  M.,  Elizabeth  Cocksall,  widow,  was  found 
to  have  owned  Babwell  next  Bury  St.  Edmunds,  being  the  site  of  the  Franciscan  Monastery,  called 
Grey  Friars,  held  of  the  King  ;  also  a  messuage  in  Fornham  St.  Martin,  formerly  Wrights,  afterwards 
Horningolds,  and  divers  lands  and  tenements.  She  died  on  the  last  day  of  October,  1557,  John 
Boldero  of  Fornham  St.  Martin,  her  son  and  heir,  being  forty  years  of  age.

At  his  Inquisition  post  mortem,  George  Boldero,  gentleman,  Margaret  Inman’s  first  husband, 
who  died  8th  Nov.  1609,  was  found  to  have  held  a  tenement  and  land  in  Bury  St.  Edmunds, 
the  site  of  Babwell  Friary,  and  lands  in  Fornham  All  Saints  and  Westley.  George  Boldero,  his  son 
and  heir,  afterwards  of  Ixworth,  was  then  aged  eleven  years  and  four  months.  For  the  inscription 
on  his  brass  in  St.  Mary’s  Church,  Bury  St.  Edmunds,  see  below.

I,  Edmund  Boldero,  Master  of  Jesus  Colledge  in  Cambridge  doe  this  nine  and  twentyeth 
day  of  March,  1679,  make  this  my  last  Will  and  Testament.  Imprimis  1  doe  declare  that  I 
looke  for  salvation  only  by  the  merritts  of  my  blessed  Redeemer,  trusting  through  his  pretious 
death  to  obtaine  mercy  and  pardon  of  my  sinnes.  And  in  his  hands  I  comend  my  soule  who 
dyed  for  all  men.  I  will  that  my  body  be  decently  buried  in  Jesus  Colledge  Chappell  where  I 
will  that  my  executor  shall  lay  a  stone  of  blacke  marble  with  this  Inscription,  Quod  super  est 
de  est,  sed  resurgam.  I  giue  to  Jesus  Colledge  Library  my  bookes  in  the  Colledge  and  at 
Snaylwell  Parsonage,  to  be  sett  apart  by  themselves,  as  a  testimony  of  the  respect  I  had  for 
that  Society.  To  my  neece  Jane  Colman  threescore  pounds  for  the  binding  out  each  of  her  two 
youngest  children,  Henry  and  Francis  Muriel  Colman,  apprentices.  To  the  towne  of  Glemsford  in

succeed.  To  the  towne  of  Snaylwell  for  the  good  of  the  poore  ffive  pounds.  I  give  Mr  John  Lord,

Edmund  Boldero,  the  seventh  son  of  John  Boldero  and  Mary  Tillott,  his  wife,  was  born  at 
Bury  St.  Edmunds,  in  1608  ;  educated  at  Ipswich  School;  admitted  to  a  Fellowship  of  Pembroke 
Hall,  Cambridge  in  1631,  when  he  took  the  degree  of  M.A.  ;  became  Curate  of  St.  Laui'ence, 
Ipswich,  1643  ;  was  ejected  from  his  Fellowship  during  the  Commonwealth,  suffering  much  for  the 
lloyalist  cause.  On  the  Restoration  he  was  created  D.D.  by  royal  mandate.  He  was  Chaplain  to 
Bishop  Wren,  who  presented  him  to  the  Rectories  of  Glemsford,  Westerfield,  and  Harkstead,  and 
afterwards  nominated  him,  in  1663,  to  the  Mastership  of  Jesus  College,  Cambridge,  which  he  held 
with  Glemsford  and  the  Rectory  of  Snailwell  in  Cambridgeshire.  He  was  Vice-Chancellor  of  the 
University  in  1668  and  1674.  For  the  inscription  on  his  monument  in  Jesus  College  Chapel 
see  below. 


John  Boldero,  M.A.,  Rector  of  Clipston  and  Dingley  in  the  county  of  Northampton.  To  be 
buried  at  Clipston  near  my  wife,  or  in  Ixworth  church  near  the  grave  of  my  dear  father,  in  case 
I  should  die  in  Suffolk,  To  my  nephew  John  Boldero,  Rector  of  Woolpit  in  Suffolk,  sixty  pounds. 
To  my  niece  Elizabeth  Boldero,  who  lived  with  me  some  years,  two  hundred  pounds.  To  my  nieces 
Anne  Wright,  Mary  Kent  and  Jane  Paine,  widow.  To  Mrs  Elizabeth  Gerard  the  daughter  of  my 
late  wife  (her  late  husband  went  to  reside  at  Coventry)  and  to  her  daughter  Sarah  Oakley.  To  my 
niece  Ann  Boldero  of  Ixworth  one  hundred  pounds.  To  my  niece  Frances  Griffin  fifty  pounds  for 
her  own  separate  use.  To  the  poor  of  Dingley  twenty  two  pounds.  To  my  said  niece  Elizabeth 
Boldero  my  great  silver  waiter  and  my  own  picture  in  the  great  parlour  at  Dingley,  and  to 
Frances  Gerard  her  mother’s  picture.  To  my  sister  MrB  Esther  Boldero  ten  pounds  for  mourning. 
To  the  eldest  child  of  my  nephew  Thomas  Cooke,  deceased,  five  pounds.  To  Mr  Nathaniel  Gerard. 
To  my  nephew  Roger  Boldero  of  Ixworth  and  his  heirs  my  lands  in  Ixworth,  formerly  my  late 
uncle’s,  John  Godbold.  To  my  nephew  George  Boldero  of  Ixworth  and  the  said  Roger  Boldero  his 
brother  my  farm  &c.  in  Old  Weston  and  other  lauds  in  the  county  of  Huntingdon.  The  said 
George  and  Roger  Boldero  to  be  executors.  Dated  the  first  of  May  1749.  Proved  1st  August 
1751  by  George  and  Roger  Boldero.  P.C.C.  228  Busby. 

We  learn  from  his  monument  in  the  nave  of  Ixworth  Church,  that  John  Boldero,  formerly 
Fellow  of  Christ  College,  Cambridge,  had  been  Rector  of  Clipston  and  Dingley  for  nearly  forty 
years.  He  died  on  the  12th  of  May,  1751,  aged  77  years.

Armorial  fterittgs. 

The  Arms  of  Garneys  of  Kenton,  as  tricked  in  Marl.  MS.  1560,  are  quarterly  of  twelve : — 

1.  Garneys. — Argent,  a  chevron  engrailed,  Azure,  between  three  escallops,  Sable. 

2.  Ramsey. — Gules,  three  rams’  heads  cabosed,  Argent. 

3.  Wellysham. —  Sable,  two  bars,  Or,  in  chief  three  cinquefoils  of  the  Second. 

4.  Kenton. — Sable,  a  chevron  between  three  cinquefoils,  Or. 

5.  Francis. — Gules,  a  chevron  engrailed,  Ermine,  between  three  “  facons  ”  rising,  Argent, 

beaked  and  membred,  Or. 

6.  Deneston. — Azure,  two  lions  passant  guardant,  Or. 

7.  Wanton. — Argent,  on  a  chevron,  Sable,  a  cross-crosslet  of  the  field. 

8.  Suliard. — Argent,  a  chevron,  Gules,  between  three  pheons,  Sable. 

9.  Hungate. — Gules,  a  chevron  between  three  “houds  seant,”  Argent. 

10.  Bacon. — Azure,  three  boars  passant,  Or. 

11.  Antingham. — Sable,  a  bend,  Argent. 

12.  Baynard. — Sable,  a  fesse  between  two  chevrons,  Or. 

With  this  tricking,  the  drawings  of  the  Garneys  shield,  in  Marl.  MS.  1820,  are  in 

substantial  agreement,  but  Wanton’s  cross-crosslet  is  fitchee  and  Hungate’s  chevron  is  engrailed. 

The  crest  is  a  cubit  arm  erased,  grasping  a  scimitar  embrued,  all  proper.  In  Marl.  MS. 
1820,  fo.  51b,  the  scimitar  is  liilted,  Or.  The  latter  MS.  (fo.  43,)  gives  a  second  crest  for 

Garneys,  viz : — A  mermaid,  Argent,  crined  and  finned,  Or,  holding  a  comb  of  the  second  in  her 
dexter  hand . 

The  following  note  appended  to  the  tricking  in  Hall.  MS.  1560,  explains  some  of  the 
quarterings. 

Thomas  Bacon  was  the  sonn  and  heire  of  John  Bacon  of  Baconsthorpe  in  Norff.  esqr  and 
of  Margerett  his  wife,  daughter  and  heire  of  Bob.  Baynard  of  Speccishall  in  Suff,  esqr,  wch  John 

Bacon  was  the  sonn  and  heire  of  Roger  sonn  and  heire  of  S’’  Thomas  Bacon  and  AUice  his  ivife 

daughter  and  heire  Sr  Barthelmew  Antingham  Knt. 

Marl.  MS.  1820,  has  also  an  achievement  for  “  John  Garneys  of  Kenton,”  evidently 
meaning  John  Garneys  of  Mendlesham,  whose  mother  was  the  heiress  of  Toppesfield,  viz.  Quarterly 
of  nine,  1  to  7  as  before.  8.  Toppesfield,  Gules,  on  a  chevron,  Ermine,  three  martlets,  Sable ; 
and  9.  Church,  Sable,  on  a  fesse  between  three  fleurs-de-lys,  Argent,  as  many  escallops,  Gules. 

Ample  pedigrees  of  Garneys  were  recorded  in  the  Suffolk  Visitations,  in  1561,  1612  and 
1664.  The  Davy  MSS.  give  fifty-eight  closely  written  pages  of  Garneys’  wills,  escheats,  deeds  and 
monumental  inscriptions,  contributed  for  the  most  part  by  the  late  Thomas  Bond,  Esq.,  of  Tyneham, 
Wareham,  a  descendant  of  the  family.

Richard  Garneys  (see  page  190)  built  Boyland  Hall  in  Morningthorpe,  Norfolk,  where  so  many  of  the  family  were  buried,  in  1571. 
Over  the  portal  he  placed  the  full  coat  of  Garneys,  with  the  Toppesfield  and  eight  other  quarterings,  supported  by  two  mermaids,  and 
in  the  windows  was  his  motto,  “ffiolJbES  ©race  ©afaerne  ©ariUJJS.”  Nicholas  Garneys,  his  kinsman  and  heir,  erected  Redisliam  Hall, 
also  during  the  reign  of  Queen  Elizabeth,  a  fine  old  mansion,  displaying  the  Garneys  shield,  quarterly  of  twelve  (see  page  189).  The 
Hedenham  monuments  have  quarterly  of  sixteen,  in  which  the  additions  are: — 11,  Bacon  of  Redgrave,  Gules,  on  a  chief,  Argent,  two 
mullets  of  the  first  ;  14,  Richmond  of  Hedenham,  Ermine,  on  a  chief,  Sable,  a  griffin  passant  Or;  and  15,  Paly  of  seven.  Or  and 

Sable,  on  a  chief.  Gules,  three  martlets  ;  the  sixteenth  quartering,  like  the  first,  being  Garneys,  Argent,  a  chevron  engrailed,  Azure, 
between  three  escallops,  Sable.  See  Blomefield’s  Norfolk,  v,  292.

Nicholas  Garneys  of  Little  Redsham,  co.  Suffolk,  Esqr,  30th  January  1623.  P»y  his  will  of 
this  date  orders  his  body  to  be  buried  near  the  chancel  wall  of  the  church  of  Ringesfield,  where 
a  great  marble  stone  is  to  be  laid  upon  his  grave,  and  his  name  and  his  wife’s  and  the  names 
of  air  his  children,  as  well  dead  and  living,  to  be  engraven  in  brass  and  fixed  upon  the  same. 
Mentions  that  he  had  had  eleven  children  by  his  wife  Ann,  whereof  there  were  then  living  three 
sons  and  five  daughters,  viz.  : — Charles,  Edward  and  Cleere,  Margarie,  Ann,  Margarett,  Kateren  and 
Elizabeth.  Gives  to  his  wife,  for  her  life,  the  Manor  of  Suddon  in  Kenton  (heretofore  assigned 
to  her  for  her  jointure),  also  two  hundred  pounds,  two  bed  stedds,  one  of  wallnut  tree  turned 
and  the  other  with  square  postes,  with  the  best  featherbedde,  boulsters,  pillowes,  blanketts  and 
coverletts  and  all  other  furniture  to  them  belonging,  two  pieces  of  the  best  of  his  silver  plate, 
the  bason  and  ewer  only  excepted,  one  garnishe  of  pewter,  Ac.,  Ac.  Upon  condition  that  she 
assure  and  convey  unto  his  son  Edward  Garneys,  and  after  him  to  his  son  Cleere  Garneys,  all 
such  right,  title  and  demand  as  she  shall  or  hereafter  may  have  in  the  Manors  of  Reddesham, 
and  Barsham  in  Suffolk,  and  all  other  his  lands,  &c.,  in  Reddesham  aforesaid,  Great  Reddesham, 
Ringesfield  and  Barsham,  or  near  thereunto,  to  such  use,  (fee.,  as  is  hereafter  expressed.  To  Charles 
Garneys,  his  son,  and  his  lieires  male,  the  Manors  of  Kenton,  Boyland  and  Fretton,  <fec.,  to  uses 
limited  in  certain  conveyances  thereof  made.  To  said  Charles  a  gold  ring  of  the  weight  of  half 
an  ounce  in  gold,  with  a  seale  therupon  engraven  of  his  arms,  ifec.  To  Edward  Garneys,  his 
son,  the  said  Manor  of  Redesham  and  Barsham,  with  all  other  the  lands,  Ac.,  in  Little  Redesham, 
Great  Redesham,  Ringesfield  and  Barsham,  contained  in  certain  Indentures  thereof  named  between 
him  and  Henry  Elmy  of  Rumburgh,  to  him  and  the  heirs  male  of  his  body ;  remainder  to  Cleere 
Garneys,  testator’s  son,  and  the  heirs  male  of  his  body  ;  remainder  to  testator’s  own  right  heirs 
as  in  said  conveyances  are  limited.  To  Elizabeth  Garneys,  his  grandchild,  daughter  of  John  Garneys, 
his  late  son,  forty  pounds  on  attaining  her  age  of  twenty  one  years.  To  Margery,  his  daughter, 
now  wife  of  Thomas  Smith,  Esqr,  one  juell  ring  of  the  value  of  forty  shillings.  To  Ann,  his 
daughter,  now  wife  of  Richard  Bellamy,  Gent.,  one  juell  ring  or  tablett,  value  40s.  To 
Margarett,  his  daughter,  now  wife  of  Thomas  Southall,  Gent.,  the  same.  To  Katherine,  his  daughter, 
now  wife  of  'William  Cuddon,  Gent.,  the  same.  To  Elizabeth,  his  daughter,  now  wife  of  Henry 
Rede,  Esqr  the  same.  Edward  Garneys,  his  son,  to  be  executor.  Five  pounds  to  be  distributed 
amongst  the  poor  people  who  shall  come  to  his  burial. 

By  a  Codicill,  dated  6  April  1628,  he  recites  the  death  of  Ann,  his  wife,  and  Elizabeth 
Garneys,  daughter  of  John  Garneys,  his  son.  The  legacies  to  them  to  be  void. 

Proved  22  Sept.  1628,  Cur.  Ep.  Norw. 

In  Ringsfield  churchyard,  in  a  lofty  niche  of  brick  on  the  south  wall  of  the  chancel,  is 
a  brass  plate  with  the  figures  of  Nicholas  Garneys  and  Anne,  his  wife,  their  eleven  children  kneeling 
behind  them.  These  figures  are  charged  with  their  respective  arms,  her’s  being  those  of  Clere  of 
Ormsby,  Argent,  on  a  fess  Azure,  three  eagles  displayed  Or.  The  shields,  singly  and  impaled,  are 
repeated  above,  with  the  mermaid  crest,  and  a  motto,  “  Flectar  non  frangar.”  There  are  suitable 
texts  of  scripture.  Below  is  the  inscription,  the  dates  being  left  blank — “  Here  vnder  lyeth  buried 
the  corpes  of  Nicholas  Garneys  Esquire  A  Anne  his  wife,  davghter  of  Charles  Cleere  of  Stoksbie 
Esqur,  which  Nicholas  builded  Redsham  Hall  and  deceased  the  daye  of  An0.”

The  Arms  of  Elmy  of  Rumborough,  as  represented  in  Harl.  MS.  1560,  are  gyronny  of  eight  Or  and  Sable ;  on  a  chief 
of  the  first  two  elm  leaves  Vert.  Raven's  note  book,  Harl.  MS.  1820,  has  the  same  coat  impaling  Tasburgh. 

The  Crest,  according  to  the  Barrett  MSS.,  so  frequently  quoted  by  Davy,  is  on  a  chapeau  a  tower  proper.  These  MSS. 

place  three  elm  leaves  on  the  chief.

The  fowerteenth  day  of  May  1623.  Michaell  Griggs  of  London,  gentleman.  I  will  that  my 
eldest  sonne  Michaell  Grigg  shall  have  all  my  lands  and  tenements  in  Dunstable,  Houghton  Regis, 
Kensworth  and  Codington  in  the  Countyes  of  Bedf.  and  Hertford.  To  Rechawrd  my  deare  and 
welbeloved  wife  my  messuages  in  Mauldon  in  the  said  countye  of  Bedford  for  terme  of  her  life : 
the  remainder  to  my  eldest  sonn  Michaell  Grigges  for  terme  of  his  life :  the  remainder  to  his 
eldest  sonne  Michaell  Grigges  :  and  for  want  of  issue  the  remainder  to  my  second  sonne  Robert 
Griggs :  and  for  default  of  issue  of  the  body  of  the  said  Robert  remainder  to  my  grandchild  Michaell 
Miller,  sonne  of  Sr  John  Miller,  Knight,  and  of  my  daughter  Dame  Marie  his  wife.  I  am  possessed 
of  the  rents  of  the  Manner  of  Becklings  in  the  parishes  of  Snape,  Sternefield  and  Freston,  in  the 
countye  of  Suffolk  under  a  lease  which  I  bought  in  the  name  of  my  second  sonne  Robert,  and 
likewise  of  divers  other  lands  in  Snape,  &c.,  free  and  copie.  My  said  sonne  Robert  shall  have 
said  lease  and  inheritance  immediately  after  the  decease  of  my  wife.  Messuage  in  Northampton 
to  my  wife  for  life,  the  remainder  to  my  sonne  Michaell  for  life,  remainder  to  Abraham  Griggs 

second  sonne  of  my  said  sonne  Michaell.  My  parte  of  that  capitall  messuage  called  the  Hargrowe 

in  the  parish  of  Church  Bicknell  in  the  countye  of  Warwicke,  and  all  my  other  lands  in  said 

countie  to  my  wife  for  life,  the  remainder  to  my  sonne  Michaell  Griggs  for  life,  the  remainder 

to  my  second  sonne,  and  for  want  of  issue  remainder  to  my  grandchild  Michaell  Pendleton.  To 
my  sonne  Michaell  Griggs  my  two  houses  in  Smithen  streete  in  Exeter.  And  out  of  the  same 
the  some  of  ffower  pounds  and  eight  shillinges  yearlie  for  ever  to  the  vse  of  the  poore  of 
Doddiscombsleighte  in  the  countie  of  Devon  where  I  was  nursed,  and  the  most  substantial!  of 
the  name  of  Babb,  Dudine  and  Shilstons  that  be  inhabiting  wthin  the  said  parishe  shall  bestowe 
the  same.  The  tenement  called  the  Old  Pallace  neare  the  Cathedral  Church  of  S*  Paul  to  my 
sonne  Michaell  Griggs  (part  being  in  his  tenure,  part  in  my  owne)  with  divers  shopps,  sellers, 
sobers  and  appurtenances.  Rent  due  to  the  Lord  Bishop  of  London  uppon  the  lease  by  which 
I  hold  the  same.  Other  messuages  in  Paule’s  Church  yard.  My  auntient  lease  of  two  tenementes 
in  great  Saint  Hellens  which  I  purchased  in  the  names  of  my  sonne  Anthonie,  now  deceased,  and

The  Inquisition  after  the  death  of  Michael  Grigg  was  taken  at  Amptliill  in  Bedfordshire,  on 
the  5th  of  August,  in  the  22nd  year  of  James  the  First.  He  had  died  seised  of  ten  messuages 
and  of  divers  lands  in  Dunstable  and  Houghton  Regis,  co.  Bedford,  and  of  messuages  and  lands  in 
Carrington  and  Kensworth,  co.  Hertford.  He  had  held  a  messuage  in  Maldon,  co.  Bedford,  Le 
Chequer  in  the  town  of  Northampton,  and  Hargrave  House  in  Bickenhall,  co.  Warwick.  He  had 
pui’chased  messuages  in  Exeter  on  his  marriage  with  Iiichawde  his  wife,  and  lands  in  Snape,  Freston, 
Sternefield  and  Farneham,  co.  Suffolk.  His  will  of  May  14th  1623,  is  recited  to  show  his  disposition 
of  these  properties.  He  died  on  the  15th  of  August,  21  James,  in  the  parish  of  St.  Gregory, 
London.  Richawd,  his  relict,  was  living,  and  held  the  premises  in  Snape,  Ac.  ;  Michael  Grigg,  his 
son  and  heir,  was  of  the  age  of  thirty  years  and  upwards  at  the  time  of  his  father’s  death.

In  Michaelmas  Term,  1611,  Michael  Grigges,  Gentleman,  bought  of  Barbara  Grigges  widow, 
Godfrey  Allen  and  Elizabeth  his  wife,  Robert  Smyth  and  Cecilia  his  wife,  Mary  Grigges  and 
Alice  Grigges,  two  messuages  with  gardens,  &c.,  and  one  hundred  and  twenty  two  acres  of  land  in 
Snape,  Freston,  Sternfield  and  Farnham  in  the  county  of  Suffolk.  Fine,  Mick.  9  Jas.  I. 

An  Indenture  is  entered  on  the  Recovery  Roll  of  Michaelmas  Term,  1653,  in  which  Michael 
Grigg  of  Otley,  co.  Suffolk,  Gent.,  sells  to  Benjamin  Grigg,  Citizen  and  Draper  of  London,  two 
messuages  with  lands  in  Snape,  Freston,  Sternfield  and  Farnham ;  also  messuage  and  lands  in 
Mawldon  and  Amthiil,  co.  Bedford,  formerly  the  property  of  Michael  Grigg,  Gent.,  grandfather  of  the 
vendor,  and  Hargrave  House  in  Church  Bicknell,  co.  Warwick,  with  the  lands  belonging. 

In  Hillary  Term,  1691,  Michael  Grigg,  Doctor  of  Law,  and  Barbara  his  wife  sold  to 
Robert  Haywai'd  a  messuage  and  lands  in  Snape,  Farnham  and  Sternfield,  co.  Suffolk.  Fine, 
Hill,  8  W.  &  M.

The  Arms  of  Grigg  of  Little  Bealings,  at  the  Visitation  of  Suffolk,  in  1664  ( Harl .  MS.  1085),  were  Argent,  three  lions 
passant,  in  pale,  with  a  bordure,  Azure,  and  were  identical  with  those  borne  by  Michael  Grigg,  High  Sheriff  of  Bedford,  in  1630. 
Davy,  in  his  “  Arms  of  Suffolk  Families  ”  {Add.  MS.  19,  159),  adds  a  Crest — Out  of  a  ducal  coronet,  a  dexter  hand  holding 
up  a  swan’s  head,  all  proper. 

In  the  window  of  a  room  in  the  Pied  Bull,  near  the  church  at  Islington,  on  the  ground  floor,  are  the  Arms  of  Sir  John 
Miller,  Ivnt.,  of  Islington.  Azure,  an  inescutcheon  between  four  mascles,  Or,  impaling  Grigg  of  Suffolk.  Lvsons’  “  Environs  of 
London,”  Vol.  Ill,  139. 

In  documents  relating  to  the  family,  of  the  sixteenth  and  earlier  part  of  the  seventeenth  centuries,  the  name  is  not 
infrequently  written  Griggs.

Jhmortal  Hearings. 

The  Arms  of  Gooding  of  Freston,  as  granted  by  Robert  Cooke  Clarencieux  in  1596  to  Robert 
Gooding  of  that  place,  were  Or,  a  fess  between  six  lions’  heads  erased  gules.  The  fess  is  charged 
with  a  crescent  argent  for  difference,  he  being  the  descendant  of  a  second  son  of  his  Blaxhall 
ancestor.  The  Crest  is  a  griffin  sejant  with  wings  expanded  or,  legged  and  beaked  sable,  guttee  de 
poix.  The  grant  itself  has  been  lost,  but  it  was  confirmed  at  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1612,  and 

is  depicted  on  the  margin  of  the  original  pedigree  in  the  College  of  Arms.  Hark  MS.  1820,  the 

corresponding  volume  at  the  British  Museum,  has  a  similar  shield  at  fo.  2,  with  the  words  “  Gooding 
per  Cooke,  1596,”  whilst  the  Crest  is  given  at  fo.  44b. 

In  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1664,  Hark  MS.  1085,  Richard  Gooding  of  Wherstead  has  the 
same  escutcheon,  also  with  a  crescent,  he  being  the  descendant  of  another  second  son.  It  is  assigned, 
provisionally,  to  George  Gooding  of  Debach  and  Robert  Gooding  of  Charsfield,  whose  ancestors  came 
from  Woodbridge  and  probably  from  Blaxhall,  with  a  note  implying  that  the  matter  would  be 
referred  to  Loudon  for  enquiry.  Goodwin  of  Torrington,  co.  Devon,  who  came  from  Suffolk,  bore 

the  like  ensigns  with  a  ring  on  the  fess  for  difference. 

In  the  earlier  evidences  of  this  family  the  name  is  written  “  Gooding.”  In  the  later  it  is 
often  changed  to  “Goodwin.”  In  the  will  of  Margaret  Gooding  of  Rendlesham,  1596,  it  is 

‘‘Goodwin”  in  the  transcript  and  “Gooding”  in  the  margin.  The  Shield  granted  to  Gooding  of 
Freston  in  1596  is  a  modification  of  those  ascribed  to  the  Earl  of  Kent  and  other  ancient  Godwins. 
Many  of  these  are  pictured  in  the  volume  known  as  E.D.N.  56,  in  the  College  of  Arms.  Amongst 
them  is  the  Coat  of  “  Goodwin  his  daughter  wife  to  K.  Edw:  Confes.,”  Gules,  between  two  bars  Or, 
six  lions’  heads,  three  two  and  one.

sayd  messuage,  together  with  other  messuages  in  Bury  devised  to  the  sayd  Mary  by  her  late 
vncle  Mr  Edward  Darbye,  to  bee  of  the  yeerely  value  of  one  hundred  poundes,  as  I  did  promise

Although  not  always  accurate,  this  pedigree,  written  by  a  neighbour  in  the  lifetime  of  many  of  the  parties  it  names,  is 
contemporary  evidence  of  no  mean  value.  It  will  be  noticed  that  it  gives  the  Goodwins  of  Rendham  and  Marlesford,  one  of 
whom  termed  Goodwin  of  Martlesham  Hall  his  cousin,  a  common  ancestry  with  the  rest.

By  liis  Inquisition  post  mortem,  7  James,  I.  77,  taken  at  Ipswich,  George  Gooding  was  found  to  have  been  seized  of  a 
messuage  and  divers  lands  in  Kirkton,  held  of  Anne,  the  Queen  Consort  of  James  the  First,  as  of  her  manor  of  W  altou  cum 
Trimley  and  Felixstowe  Priory,  and  also  of  lauds  in  Clopton  held  of  Sir  John  Rouse,  Knt.,  as  of  his  Manor  of  Kingshall  in 
Clopton.  He  died  at  Grundisburgh  14  January,  6  James  ;  George  Gooding,  his  son  and  heir,  being  twenty  years  of  age. 

Most  of  the  family  pictures  and  other  heirlooms  of  the  Goodwins  of  Martlesham,  Ac.  (including  a  coat  of  arms  beautifulh 
worked  in  silk  by  Mary  Edgar  wife  of  John  Goodwin  of  Hasketon),  are  now  in  the  possession  of  Mrs.  Doughty  of  Lowestoft,  widow 
of  Admiral  Fredk.  Proby  Doughty,  and  eldest  daughter  of  the  Rev.  Richard  Aldous  Arnold,  Rector  of  Ellough,  herself  a  descendant 
of  the  Goodwin  family.

Amongst  the  insignia  of  the  various  families  of  Goodwin  depicted  in  the  volume  known  as 
E.D.N.,  56,  in  the  College  of  Arms,  is  a  somewhat  remarkable  shield,  which  may  be  described  as 
Argent,  a  pale  gules  ;  in  chief  and  in  base  a  plate  between  two  fleurs  de  lys,  and  in  fess  a  delu¬ 
de  lys  between  two  plates,  all  counterchanged.  The  accompanying  Crest  is  “a  mallard  tree  vert  ; 
on  either  side  a  cony  argent  eating  the  leaves  thereof.  It  is  not  said  to  what  Goodwins  these 
arms  were  assigned,  and  no  record  of  the  grant  has  been  officially  preserved  by  the  heralds.  A 
similar  reticence  is  observed  by  Add.  MS.  26,702,  in  the  British  Museum,  which  seems  to  be  a  copy 
of  E.D.N.  56.  But  in  Harleian  MS.  1422,  an  old  and  faded  collection  of  “Grants  by  Divers  Kings 
of  Arms  tricked  by  John  Gough,”  this  shield  and  crest  are  said  to  have  been  given  to  “  Wilim 
Goodwin  of  Booking  in  com  Essex  p  Wrioth.  G.  36.  H.  8.”  A  note  has  been  appended,  apparently 
in  another  hand,  “  ffile  p  Sr  Xpof  Barkl  G.,”  together  with  an  indication  that  the  leaves  which 
the  rabbits  are  eating  are  intended  for  “  mallows.” 

There  were  many  Goodwins  of  Booking  in  the  sixteenth  and  seventeenth  centuries,  but  their 
exact  relationship  has  never  been  determined.  They  made  but  few  wills  and  the  earlier  Booking 
registers  and  manor  books  are  alike  missing.  It  is  not  improbable  that  the  Goodwins  of  Hartford 
in  Connecticut  come  of  the  same  stock.  Many  valuable  evidences  connected  with  the  Booking 
Goodwins,  including  ample  abstracts  of  the  wills  of  Sir  Thomas  Pope,  1556,  and  Anne  Rlunt,  1594, 
are  printed  in  the  “  Report  on  English  Investigations,”  contributed  by  Mr.  Henry  F.  Waters  to  the 
history  of  this  family.1  The  name  is  usually  written  “Goodwin,”  but  John  Peppys,  uncle  of 
William  Goodwin  of  Bermondsey,  in  making  his  will  in  1551,  refers  to  his  “sister  Goodinge”  and 
her  children,  and  describes  his  nephew  as  William  Godinge  als  Goodwyn.

Close  Roll,  11  Eliz.  14th  part. 

Thomas  Goodwin  was  but  eight  years  old  when  his  father  died,  and  much  of  his  inheritance 
seems  to  have  been  made  away  with  by  John  Felton,  his  mother’s  second  husband.  Goodwin  c.  Felton 
Chanc.  Proc.,  Series  II,  74,  42.  Becoming  embarrassed  in  his  circumstances  he  sold  his  lands  in 
Felsted  to  John  Fitche,  and  a  little  later  four  messuages,  four  gardens,  sixteen  acres  of  arable  land 
and  four  acres  of  woodland  in  Booking  to  one  Francis  Archer.  Fine ,  Easter,  12  Eliz.  The 
Indenture  between  Thomas  Goodwin  and  John  Fitche  is  the  last  known  document  which  mentions 
him  as  an  inhabitant  of  Booking.  By  an  interesting  coincidence  it  would  appear  that  a  John 
Goodwin  and  a  Richard  Fitche  were  churchwardens  there  in  1602.  Backing,  Inhabitants  of,  c. 
Smith,  Eliz.,  B  ifc  A,  BB,  29,  44.

By  his  will  dated  8th  March  1534  (P.C.C.  30  Hogen)  John  Smith  of  Ipswich,  Orchall-maker, 
left  his  Manor  of  Bulls  Hall  in  Bedfield  and  other  lands  to  Sir  Humphrey  Wingfield,  Sir  Thomas 
Rush  and  Ralph  Goodwin  of  Ipswich,  his  executors,  to  be  sold  by  them.  His  Inquisition  Post 
Mortem,  taken  35  H.  8,  tells  us  he  had  purchased  it  of  William  Byggot,  Gent.

We  learn  from  the  Chancery  Proceedings  in  Goodwyn  c  Skynnei,  a.d.  1600  (Eliz.  B  <k  A, 
GG.  5,  15),  that  the  testator  was  then  Messenger  in  the  Court  of  Wards,  and  that  he  had  had  the 
Patent  or  Grant  of  the  Stewardship  of  the  Manors  of  Lavenham  in  Suffolk  and  Castle  Camps  and 
Foulmer  in  Cambridgeshire  conferred  upon  him  in  the  36th  and  37th  years  of  Queen  Elizabeth  by 
Thomas  Skynner,  sometime  Lord  Mayor  of  London.  His  identity  with  Christopher  Goodwin,  the 
grandson  of  Raphe  Goodwin,  Portman  of  Ipswich,  has  yet  to  be  established.

Thomas  Spelman  of  Norwich,  geut.,  married  Cecily,  daughter  and  heir  of  .  .  .  Reedham  of  Ipswich,  gent.,  widow

Alice  and  Cicely  Reedham,  the  daughters  and  coheirs  of  .  .  .  Reedham  of  Ipswich,  were  of  tender  years  in 
1561,  Thomas  Flatman  being  their  guardian.  They  were  seized  of  lands  and  tenements  in  Ipswich  and  Bramford, 
together  with  a  messuage  and  two  hundred  acres  in  Toppesfield  and  Finchingfield,  co.  Essex,  the  evidences  of  which 
had  come  into  the  hands  of  Elizabeth  Layer,  widow.  Redham  c.  Layer,  Chancery  Proceedings,  Series  II,  155,  1. 


#oothotn  of  Cast  J&crgljolt. 


Ralph  Goodwin,  who  purchased  an  estate  at  North  Burlingham  in  Norfolk,  in  1491,  would 
seem  to  be  the  common  ancestor  of  the  Goodwins  of  North  Burlingham  and  of  East  Bergholt. 
The  manor  called  Goodwin’s  in  the  former  place  had  passed  from  the  name  before  the  35th  year  of 
Henry  VIII.  Blomefield’s  Norfolk,  VII,  22^.  Margaret,  eldest  daughter  of  Richard  Goodwin  of 
North  Burlingham,  married  there  in  1559  to  James  Keppinge  of  Freetliorpe,  was  one  of  the  next-of- 
kin  who  contested  the  will  of  John  Goodwin  of  East  Bergholt  in  1  GO  1 .  Decree,  P.C.C.  J-5  Woodhall. 
Full  abstracts  or  verbatim  copies  of  the  wills  of  Ralph  Goodwin  of  North  Burlingham,  1518,  John 
Goodwin  of  East  Bergholt,  1600,  Daniel  Goodwin  of  Yoxford,  1625,  and  John  Goodwin  of  East 
Bergholt,  1638,  with  other  valuable  evidences  bearing  on  the  history  of  the  family,  are  given  in 
“  The  Goodwins  of  Hartford,  Connecticut,”  pp.  46-56.  The  complicated  relationships  of  John 
Goodwin,  who  bequeathed  fifty  pounds  to  the  plantation  of  New  England,  are  best  explained  perhaps 
by  the  Chancery  Proceedings  in  Woodgate  c.  Goodwin,  Eliz.,  B  &  A,  Woodgate  c.  Goodwin,  Jas  I, 
P>  A  A,  and  Chaplin  c.  Woodgate,  Mitford  V,  lxxvi,  35,  which  will  probably  appear  amongst  the 
“  Genealogical  Gleanings  in  England,”  contributed  by  Mr.  Henry  F.  Waters  to  the  “  New  Eugland 
Historical  and  Genealogical  Register.”

The  Inquisition  of  Daniel  Goodwin,  the  younger  son,  who  succeeded  to  the  Manor  of  Boy  tons 
(Miscelh  Inq.  p  m.  1 6,  39),  was  taken,  long  after  his  decease,  in  the  fifteenth  year  of  King 
Charles  the  First,  He  held  most  of  the  lands  above  referred  to,  a  Thomas  Woolward  being  one 
of  his  tenants.  At  his  death  on  the  20th  of  December,  1625,  Edmund  Goodwin,  his  son  and 
heir,  was  found  to  be  ten  years  of  age. 


Will  of  ffiootifom,  1645. 

I  Edmund  Goodwyn  of  Neyland  in  the  couutie  of  Sniff  make  this  my  last  will  in  manner 
followinge.  Haveinge  alreadie  provided  with  god  for  my  soule  I  leave  my  bodie  to  bee  buried 
by  my  Executor.  I  give  vnto  Margarett  my  wife  all  my  landes  in  the  occupation  of  Richard 
Mosse  and  after  her  decease  to  my  sonne  Edmund  and  his  heires.  I  give  unto  her  all  the 

revenues  of  my  lands  and  tenements  vntill  my  sonne  Edmund  shall  attaine  to  the  age  of  one 

A  twentie  yeares,  that  out  of  the  profitts  maie  bee  gatherd  ffiue  hundred  poundes  which  I  give 
for  my  daughter  Maries  portion,  to  be  paied  at  one  and  twentie  yeares  of  age  or  daie  of 
marriage,  and  one  hundred  poundes  vnto  my  sonne  Daniell.  I  giue  to  my  sonne  Daniell  all  my 
lands  and  tenements  in  the  occupation  of  James  Hedge  and  John  Woolward,  hee  to  enter  the 
same  at  the  age  of  one  and  twentie  yeares,  and  in  the  meanetime  my  wife  to  have  the  profitts 
thereof.  To  my  sonne  Edmund  all  my  other  landes  and  tenements  formerly  not  mentioned,  to  enter 

the  same  at  one  and  twentie  yeares  of  age.  I  make  my  beloved  wife  my  sole  execuP.  I  would 

have  my  wife  looke  to  the  traineinge  vpp  of  my  children  in  the  feare  of  god,  teachinge  of  them 
till  theire  severall  ages  aforesaid  out  of  my  said  landes  and  tenements.  I  desire  that  my  worthie 
freindes  Natliainell  Bacon  Esqr  and  Colonell  Brampton  Gurdon  Esqr  would  bee  pleased  to  see 
this  will  performed.  And  that  their  love  in  so  doinge  may  bee  considered  not  in  a  sparinge 
waie  but  to  theire  content.  This  tenth  daie  of  June  1645.  Probatum  vndecimo  die  ffebruarij 
1645  Juramento  Margarete  Goodwin  relicte.  P.C.C.  13  Twisse.

The  paternity  of  William  Goodwin,  the  New  England  emigrant  of  1632,  has  not,  as  yet, 
been  definitely  ascertained,  but  it  is  probable  that  he  came  from  Braintree  or  Booking,  which 
together  form  one  long  street  in  the  county  of  Essex.  He  was  one  of  the  so-called  “  Braintree 
Company,”  which  Mr.  Hooker  followed  to  the  western  world.  Men  from  Braintree  were  amongst 
his  fellow  voyagers.  His  brother,  Ozias  Goodwin,  had  married  a  Braintree  woman.  A  William 
Goodwin  of  Booking,  who  may  well  have  been  himself,  was  son-in-law,  in  1617,  to  Robert 
White  of  Messingfu  Indeed,  Goodwins  in  some  number  had  lived  in  Booking  for  generations,  and 
had  continued  to  reside  there  until  his  day.  There  is  a  remarkable  coincidence,  too,  connected 
with  the  Christian  name  of  his  brother — Ozias.  Its  use  is  singularly  rare  ;  but  it  seems  to  have 
been  affected,  so  far  as  Suffolk  and  Essex  arc  concerned,  by  people  who  had  some  kind  of 
connection  with  Booking.  In  1618,  Ozias  Adams  was  owner  of  a  messuage  called  Potter’s  in 
Booking  which  had  descended  to  him  from  his  father.1  In  1663,  there  died  at  Booking  a  Richard 
Merrells,  apparently  of  the  same  stock  as  Ozias  Merrells,  the  father,  and  Ozias  Merrells,  the  son, 
of  the  Sudbury  family  of  that  name,  whilst  the  names  of  Ozias  Paske,  John  Adams  and  Richard 
Merrells  occur  in  significant  juxtaposition  as  kinsmen  and  devisees  of  Thomas  Hammond  of 
Hawkedon  in  1670.  A  township,  some  of  whose  inhabitants  were  surnamed  Goodwin,  and  others 
christened  Ozias,  is  not  unlikely,  one  would  think,  to  have  produced  the  Ozias  Goodwin  whose 
descendants  helped  to  people  Connecticut. 


Will  of  Eokrt  Woo&hmrft,  1640. 

The  seaven  &  twentieth  day  of  May,  in  the  sixteenth  yeare  of  our  Sovereigne  Lord  Charles, 
by  the  Grace  of  God  of  England  Ac.  King  :  I  Robert  Woodward  of  Brayntree  in  the  county  of 
Essex  doe  make  A  ordayne  this  my  last  will.  I  commend  my  soule  into  the  hands  of  God,  by  the 

merits  of  Jesus  Christ  my  blessed  redeemer,  in  assured  hope  to  inherit  yl  immortall  kingdome 

prepared  for  all  his  Ellect  people.  I  giue  unto  Mr  Collins  my  faithfull  paster  twenty  shillings.  Vnto 
my  sister  Rachel  Clay  the  wife  of  Myles  Clay  of  Brayntree  twenty  shillings.  Vnto  my  father  in 
law  Edward  Clay  my  best  cloake.  I  give  A  bequeath  unto  my  daughter  Mary  Goodwin,  the  wife 
-of  Ozias  Goodwin  now  in  New  England  tenne  shillings.  Unto  my  sonne  John  Woodward  tenne 
pounds  at  his  age  of  one  A  twenty  yeare.  The  rest  of  my  goods  I  giue  to  Joane  Woodward  my 

wife,  and  doe  appointe  the  said  Jone  sole  A  alone  executrixe.  And  intreat  my  good  friend  and 

brother  Myles  Clay  to  bee  my  suprovisor.  Probate  fuit  apud  Brancktree  xi  Julij  1640  iuramto 
extricis.

The  will  of  Thomas  Goodwyn  of  litle  Stonham  in  the  county  of  Suff.  Esquier  written 
with  his  owne  hand.  I  bequeath  my  soule  into  the  hands  of  my  gracious  God  in  Christ  J  esus. 
I  doe  charge  my  executor  as  he  shall  aunswere  it  at  the  dreadful  day  of  Judgment  to  pay  all  my 
iust  debts  to  one  penny.  If  my  executor  cannot  pay  my  debts  within  a  convenient  tyme  hee  shall 
make  sale  of  my  landes  in  Stoweupland  and  Gipping  as  also  my  lease  in  Earlstonham.  I  geue  vnto 
John  Goodwyn  my  sonne  my  houses  and  lands  in  East  Tuddenham  &  Coulton  within  the  county 
of  Norff.  I  geue  vnto  Anne  Goodwyn  my  daughter  six  hundred  pounds  out  of  the  proffitts  of  my 
Mannor  of  S6  Omers  in  Burwell  within  the  county  of  Cambridge.  Vnto  Bartram  Goodwyn  my 
sonne  the  advowson  of  Stanningfeld  within  the  county  of  Suff.  Vnto  Edward  Goodwyn  my  sonne 
my  interest  in  the  fishing  voyage  with  the  right  honourable  Phillipp,  Earle  of  Pembrocke,  the  said 
Edward  making  payment  of  the  residue  of  the  money  which  remaynes  behind  of  my  vnderwrighting. 
Vnto  Ambrose  my  sonne  all  the  right  in  the  Salt  pannes  or  works  which  I  have  purchased  at  the 
South  &  North  Shields  within  the  counties  of  Durham  &  Northumberland  as  alsoe  my  interest  in 
the  company  of  the  Saltmakers,  provided  that  he  doe  pay  vnto  my  daughter  Anne  in  increase  of  her 
porcon  formerly  geven  vnto  her  the  some  of  flower  hundred  poundes.  I  geue  vnto  Dorothy 
Rookwood  my  daughter  three  hundred  poundes.  Vnto  Bartram  my  sonne  twoe  hundred  poundes. 
Vnto  Edward  my  sonne  five  hundred  poundes.  I  geue  vnto  Thomas  Watson  my  old  servant  twenty 
nobles  a  yeere  during  his  life  out  of  my  lease  in  Poyers  in  Mendelsham  hopeing  he  wilbe  a  faithfull 
servant  vnto  my  sonne  as  hee  hath  bene  vnto  mee.  Vnto  the  children  of  George  Buckenham,  late  of 
Bradfeild  St  Clare’s,  ffortie  pounds,  in  performance  of  a  trust  by  their  ffather  reposed  in  mee.  I  doe 
ordaine  Ambrose  Goodwyn  my  sonne  my  sole  executor.  Alsoe  I  doe  make  my  especiall  frendes 
Harbottle  Wingfield  Esquire  and  John  Sheppard  of  Mendelsham  gent  to  bee  the  Supervisors  and 
doe  geue  to  each  of  them  tenn  poundes  to  buy  them  a  peece  of  plate  in  remembrance  of  my 
loue  to  them.  Last  I  geue  vnto  Mr  Wragg  the  Minister  of  Mendelsham  ffive  poundes  to  preach 
at  my  buryall  if  God  call  mee  within  the  the  county  of  Suff.  I  subscribed  my  hand  this  thre 
&  twentieth  day  of  January  1635.  If  it  please  the  Lord  to  bring  mee  back  againe  from  my 
iourney  I  entend  to  make  this  my  will  more  perfect.  Probatum  25  Aprilis  1638,  Juramento 
Ambrosii  Goodwyn  filij.  P.C.C.  39  Lee. 

By  his  Inquisition  post  mortem  (Escli.  14  Car.  3,  80),  taken  at  Eye  on  the  tenth  of  September 
in  the  fourteenth  year  of  Charles  the  First,  Thomas  Goodwin  was  found  to  have  been  seized  of  the 
Manors  of  Stoneliam  Jernegan  and  Mendlesham  in  Suffolk,  Belhouse  in  North  Tuddenham  in  Norfolk, 
Tomers  alias  Thomers  in  Cambridgeshire,  and  Appleton  super  Wiske  in  Yorkshire.  He  died  so 
siezed  on  the  third  of  April,  1638,  Ambrose  Goodwin,  his  son  and  heir,  being  then  aged  forty  years 
and  upwards.

Confirmation  of  Jlrnts  to  Joint  ®aulor,  1572. 

To  all  and  singular  as  well  nobles  and  gentills  as  others  to  whom  these  presentes  shall  come 
Robert  Cooke  Esquier  alias  Clarencieulx  principall  lierehault  and  Kinge  of  armes  of  the  Sowth  Este 
and  West  partes  of  this  Realme  of  Englande  from  the  River  of  Treute  southwards  sendith  greeting. 
Wheras  aunciently  from  the  beginninge  the  valiaunt  and  vertuous  actes  of  worthie  persons  have  been 
comended  to  the  worlde  with  sondry  monumentes  and  remembrances  of  their  good  desertes,  Emongst 
the  which  the  chefest  and  most  vsuall  hath  ben  the  bearinge  of  signes  in  shildes  called  Armes 
which  are  euident  demonstracions  of  prowes  and  valoir  diversly  distributed  accordinge  to  the  qualities 
and  desertes  of  the  persons  order  as  it  was  most  prudently  deuised  in  the  beginninge  to  st-irre  and 
kindell  the  hartes  of  men  to  the  imitacion  of  vertuc  and  noblenes.  Euen  so  hath  the  same  ben 
and  yet  is  continually  obserued  to  the  ende  that  such  as  liaue  don  comendable  sendee  to  their 
Prynce  or  Contry  either  in  warre  or  peace  maye  bothc  receaue  due  honor  in  their  lines  &  also 
deriue  the  same  successively  to  their  posteritie  after  them.  And  beinge  required  of  John  le  Talor 
of  London  Esquier  to  make  searche  in  the  regesters  and  recordes  of  my  Office  for  the  auncient 
Armes  belonginge  to  that  name  and  familie  whereof  he  is  descended,  wheruppon  I  have  at  his 
request  made  searche  accordingly  so  that  findingc  the  true  and  perfect  descent  I  coulde  not  without 
his  great  preiudice  assigne  vnto  him  any  other  than  those  whiche  are  to  him  descended  from  his 
anneestors.  That  is  to  saye  quarterly,  in  the  firstc  for  Talor  sables  a  lion  passant  siluer,  in  the 
seconde  for  Beniclere  golde  a  lion  rampant  regardant  gules  a  coller  siluer,  in  the  thirde  for  Sely  siluer 
a  cheueron  gules  betwen  thre  egles  displaied  sables,  the  laste  as  the  firste.  And  for  that  I  finde 
no  Creaste  vnto  the  same,  as  commonly  to  all  auncient  Armes  there  belongeth  none,  I  haue  giueu 
vnto  him  by  waye  of  encrease  for  his  Creaste  or  Coguoisance  vppon  his  healme  on  a  wreath  siluer  and 
sables  an  Ownce  standinge  in  proper  cooler  manteled  gules  dowbled  siluer  as  more  plainly  apperith 
depicted  in  this  margent.  The  whiche  Armes  and  Creaste  and  euery  parte  and  parcell  thereof  I  the 
saide  Clarencieulx  Kinge  of  Armes  by  power  and  aucthoritie  to  my  Office  annexed  and  grawnted  by 
Letters  patentes  vnder  the  great  seale  of  Englande  to  ratifie  confirme  and  allowe  to  the  saide  John 
le  Talor  Esquier  and  to  his  posteritie  with  their  due  differences  and  they  the  same  to  vse  beare  and 
shewe  in  Shilde  cote  armour  or  othervvaies  at  his  and  their  liberty  and  pleasure  without  impediment 
let  or  interuption  of  any  person  or  persons.  In  witnes  whereof  I  the  saide  Clarenciewlx  Kinge  of 
Armes  have  sett  hereunto  my  handc  and  seale  of  Office  the  xxth  day  of  Juli  in  a°  1572  and  in  the 
fourteenth  yere  of  the  reigne  of  owre  souereigne  Lady  Elizabeth  by  the  grace  of  God  Queno  of 
Englande  franco  and  Irelande  defendor  of  the  faith,  Ac. 

Rob°t  Cooke  alias  Clarencieulx,  Roy  Darmes.

I  Henry  Farnham  Burke  Esquire,  Somerset  Herald  of  Arms  and  Genealogist  of  the  Most 
Illustrious  Order  of  Saint  Patrick,  do  hereby  certify  and  declare  that  the  Armorial  Bearings  above 
depicted,  namely,  Arms — Quarterly  of  six,  1st  and  6th  azure  a  saltire  parted  and  fretty  between  four 
martlets  argent  (for  Smith  of  Kilburn),  2nd  gules  on  a  chevron  or  between  three  bezants  as  many 
crosses  patee  fi  tehee  sable,  in  the  centre  chief  point  (for  cadency)  a  martlett  or  (for  Smith  of 
Withcote),  3rd  sable  a  lion  passant  argent  (for  le  Talor),  4th  or  a  lion  rampant  guardant  gules 
•collared  argent  (for  Beniclere),  5th  argent  a  chevron  gules  between  three  eagles  displayed  sable  (for 
Sely).  Crests — 1st  (Smith  of  Kilburn)  in  front  of  a  mount  a  serpent  nowed  thereon  an  owl  all 
proper,  2nd  (Smith  of  Withcote)  a  cubit  arm  erect  vested  per  pale  or  and  azure  cuffed  argent,  the 
hand  proper  holding  a  griffin’s  head  erased  of  the  second  beaked  gold,  charged  on  the  n.eck  (for 
cadency)  with  a  martlet  of  the  last,  Motto,  Coenobio  Salvus — do  of  right  belong  and  appertain  unto 
the  descendants  of  Samuel  Montgomery  Smith,  late  of  Paradise  House,  Kilburn,  deceased,  and  are 
duly  registered  to  them  in  the  Records  of  the  Herald’s  College,  London,  as  witness  my  hand  this 
twentieth  day  of  February  1891.  H.  Farnham  Burke,  Somerset.

Sir  Thomas  Freke  of  Ewern  Courtney,  son  of  Robert  Freke,  Esq.,  one  of  the  Tellers  of  the 

Exchequer  in  the  reigns  of  Henry  VIII  and  Queen  Elizabeth,  was  a  person  of  considerable  note 

in  the  county  of  Dorset.  The  parish  church  of  Ewern  Courtney  (a  place  more  generally  known 
as  Shroton)  was  rebuilt  by  him  in  1614.  It  is  a  typical  specimen  of  the  church  architecture  of 
the  period.  The  burial  place  of  the  Frekes  is  at  the  higher  end  of  the  north  aisle  and  is 
enclosed  by  wooden  screens  curiously  carved  with  corbel  heads  and  pinnacles  and  scroll  work,  the 
cornice  of  one  of  which  supports  the  Arms  of  Taylor  of  Lidgate.  Within,  a  stately  monument 
commemorates  Sir  Thomas,  who  died  in  1633,  and  Dame  Elizabeth.  A  long  and  eloquent 
inscription  records  their  virtues.  On  their  escutcheon — Freke,  Sable  two  bars  Or,  in  chief  two 
mullets  of  the  same,  impales  Taylor  quartering  Beniclcre  and  Cely.  The  Crest  is  a  bull’s  head 
eouped  Sable,  horned  Or.  The  matches  of  their  numerous  children  are  indicated  by  other  shields. 
There  is  a  full  pedigree  of  the  Frekes  in  Hutchins’  “History  of  Dorset,”  vol.  iv.  From  Ralph 
Freke,  a  younger  son  of  Sir  Thomas,  descend  the  Hussey-Frekes  of  Hannington  in  Wiltshire.  It 
was  William  Freke,  brother  of  Sir  Thomas,  who  became  the  ancestor  of  the  Frekes,  Baronets  of 
West  Bilncy  in  Norfolk,  and  of  the  Evans-Frekes,  Barons  Carbury.

Richard  Wybeard  of  High  Ownger  in  the  county  of  Essex,  gentleman,  the  seaventeenth 
September  1607.  I  bequeath  to  almighty  god  my  soule  which  I  most  humbly  beseech  his  heavenly 
maiestie  even  for  his  sonne  Christe  Jesus  his  sake  to  make  partaker  of  eternall  blessedness.  My  body 
to  be  buried  in  some  convenient  place  within  the  church  of  Highe  Ownger.  To  John  Wiberd  myne 
eldest  sonne  the  somtue  of  tenn  poundes.  And  to  my  sonne  Lawrence  tenn  poundes.  And  to  my 
sonne  William  thirty  poundes.  And  to  my  sonne  Roberte  forty  shillinges.  And  to  my  daughter  Mary 
the  wife  of  Roberte  Webster  I  giue  live  markes.  And  to  Catherine  wife  to  William  Habell  five 
markes.  To  Jeremy  Wibeard  my  sonne  one  hundred  markes  when  he  shall  come  to  the  full 
age  of  twenty  and  six  yeares,  said  Jeremy  to  enter  into  bond  not  to  take  to  wife  one  Margaret 
Hammond  the  daughter  of  Mathewe  Hamond  and  his  cozen  germaine.  To  Edward  Wibeard  my 
youngest  sonne  fiftie  poundes  at  his  ago  of  twenty  and  sixe  yeares.  Unto  Jeremy  my  greate 
guilte  salte  after  the  decease  of  Margaret  my  wiefe.  To  my  daughter  Joane  Somibaneke  six 
angelles.  To  Margaret  Hamond  my  kinswoman  and  servaunte  twenty  shillinges.  To  old  Mary 
my  maide  twenty  shillinges.  The  rest  of  my  goodes,  my  landes  Ac.  I  giue  to  Margaret  my  wife 
whome  I  doe  name  executrix.  And  I  doe  appoynte  Charles  Somibaneke  Doctor  of  Diuinity  my 
sonne  in  lawe  overseer.  Probatum  nono  die  Maij  1610  juramento  Margarete  Wibeard  relicte.

Ufflet,  jun.,  conveyed  the  Manor  of  Titsall  in  Herringfleet  to  John  Hammond,  29  Jan.  1631.  It

1650,  Richard  Hammond  of  Ditchingham,  co.  Norfolk,  Gent.,  sold  this  manor  to  Thomas  Meadow, 
Alderman  of  Great  Yarmouth.

The  Hammonds  of  Ellingham  by  Bungay,  although  Norfolk  gentry,  descended  from  Suffolk,  resided  near  the  Suffolk  border) 
and  held  Suffolk  Manors.  Their  pedigree  from  the  Norfolk  Visitations  of  1613  (Harl.  MS.  1449  and  1552)  and  1664  (College  of 
Arms)  is  printed  in  italics.  Their  Arms  (Harl.  MS.  1449  and  Bysshe’s  Norfolk  Visitatiou,  1664)  were  Argent,  on  a  chevron,  Sable 
three  martlets  of  the  field.  Crest : — On  a  wreath  Or  and  Gules,  out  of  a  ducal  coronet  of  the  first,  an  elephant’s  head  Argent, 

tusked  and  eared  Or.

Thomas  Heigham  sold  lands  in  Hawkedon,  Stansfield,  Somerton  and  Brockley  to  John 
Andrews  in  the  first  year  of  Edward  the  Sixth.  Fine,  Mich.  1,  E.  0.  In  the  second  year 
of  Edward  the  Sixth,  John  Cawston  and  John  Andrews  held  the  Manor  of  Cresseners  in 
Hawkedon  of  the  Honour  of  Clare  by  the  service  of  half  a  Knight’s  fee.  Rental  of  the  Honour 
of  Clare  in  the  Dutchy  Court  of  Lancaster ,  quoted  by  Davy.  In  the  third  year  of  Queen  Elizabeth, 
John  Cawston  assured  Cresseners  to  Anne  Hammond,  his  daughter,  and  Thomas  Hammond,  her 
husband.  His  will,  Arch.  Sndb.,  dated  8  Feb.  1560,  was  proved  in  1564.
