1,  Philip  Hamond  of  Hawkedon  in  the  county  of  Suffolk,  Esquire,  confirm  to  Elizabeth  my 
wife  my  estate  called  Hawkedon  Hall  (according  to  the  true  intent  of  my  son  Philip  Hamond’s 

articles  of  marriage)  now  in  my  own  occupation,  with  a  liberty  of  living  in  the  said  house.  T0 

Philip  Hamond,  my  eldest  son,  the  Little  House  upon  Hawkedon  Green ;  he  to  suffer  Elizabeth 
my  wife  to  recieve  rents  during  her  life,  the  better  to  enable  her  to  pay  my  cosen  Anne  Barker 
her  annuity  of  ten  pounds  a  year  and  her  interest  money  of  sixty  pounds.  Said  Philip  to  pay 
his  youngest  sister  Anne  Hamond  forty  pounds  after  wives  death.  To  my  youngest  daughter  Anne 
and  her  heirs  for  ever  ffarme  in  Boxted  Street,  with  lands  in  Boxted,  Hartest  A  Stansted.  Unto 
said  son  Philip  Hamond  the  eight  pounds  a  year  payable  by  my  son  Mr  John  Keye  out  of  the 
Mote  ffarm  in  Boxted  Ac.  Wife  to  pay  to  my  son  John  Hamond  thirty  shillings  a  year,  and  to 
my  sister  Anne  Pells  of  North  Glemham,  widow,  eight  pounds  a  year.  Goods  to  wife.  To  be

youngest  daughter  Anne  Hamond  to  be  sole  executrix.  10  Nov.  1731.  Probate  21  Nov.  1735.

The  Arms  of  Hammond,  as  represented  on  the  hatchments,  Ac.,  in  the  churches  of  Hawkedon 

and  Boxsted,  are  Per  pale  gules  and  azure,  three  demi-lions  passant  guardant  or  ;  and  the  Crest, 

a  wolf’s  head  erased  quarterly  or  and  azure.  The  greater  part  of  the  pedigree  which  follows  is 
taken  from  the  Records  of  the  College  of  Arms.

This  pedigree  is  founded  upon  the  Chancery  Proceedings  in  Payton  contra  Hamond,  Q.  Elizabeth,  B  and  A,  P.p.  14.  41, 
dated  12  June  1588.  The  complainants  are  Adam  Payton  of  Bury  St.  Edmunds,  Margaret  Bright  of  Bury,  widow,  Richard  Wilson 
of  Rattlesden,  clerk,  and  Margery,  his  wife,  Simon  Langham  of  Bury  and  Rose,  his  wife,  Clement  Hynds  of  Ely  and  Elizabeth, 
Ids  wife,  and  Richard  Hancock  of  Ely  and  Sibill,  his  wife  ;  said  Adam  Payton,  Margaret  Bright,  Margery  Wilson,  Rose  Langham, 
Elizabeth  Hynds  and  Sibill  Hancock  being  children  of  one  William  Payton  of  Risby,  who  made  his  will  6  Sept.  1556.  The 
principal  defendants  are  Thomas  Hammond  and  Ann,  his  wife,  the  only  child  of  Thomas  Paytou,  deceased,  eldest  son  and  heir 
of  William  Payton,  the  testator,  and  brother  to  the  complainants.  The  suit  relates  to  lands,  &c.,  in  Risby,  Bury  St.  Edmunds) 
and  Little  Saxham,  settled  by  testator  upon  Johan,  his  wife.  It  is  stated  that  he  had  six  sons  and  seven  daughters  by  the 
said  Johan,  who  survived  him  one  and  tlxirty  years.  Their  names,  as  recited  in  the  proceedings,  are  given  above.

The  above  differs  in  many  respects  from  the  pedigree  given  by  Gage  in  his  “History  of  Thingoe,”  which  is  founded  upon 
the  information  of  Sir  Francis  Thomas  Hammond.  Sir  Thomas  bore  as  Arms,  Quarterly  1st,  Argent,  on  a  chevron  Sable  between  three 
ogresses,  each  charged  with  a  martlet  of  the  field,  three  escallops  Or,  all  within  a  bordure  engrailed  Vert ;  for  Hammond  (the  will  of 

his  ancestor,  in  1638,  having  been  sealed  with  a  chevron  between  three  ogresses)  :  2d,  Bendy  Or  and  Azure,  for  Asty  ;  3d,  Checquy 

Or  and  Gules,  a  canton  Ermine,  for  Rayne :  and  4th,  Argent,  on  a  chevron  Sable,  threee  crosses  patee  Or,  for  Benson.  Crest. 

An  eagle  Sable,  bsuant  out  of  a  ducal  crown  Or,  infiled  with  a  rose  proper.  It  is  difficult  to  reconcile  these  quarterings,  and 

indeed  Gage’s  pedigree  itself,  with  the  data  afforded  by  the  wills,  deeds,  licenses,  Ac.,  upon  which  the  present  genealogy  is  based.

I  Edward  Hamond  the  elder  of  Ipswich,  marriner,  being  through  ye  rich  mercy  of  God  in 
perfect  health  mind  and  memory  make  this  my  last  will  and  testament  in  manner  and  forme

pounds  at  day  of  marriage  &c.  and  my  parte  of  the  sliipp  called  the  Patriarke.  Vnto  Thomazine 
my  wife  while  she  remaines  my  widdowe  the  vse  of  my  personall  estate,  shipping,  goods  &c.  for 
the  educating  and  bringing  up  my  children.  After  her  decease  the  house  I  dwell  in  to  Edward 
my  sonne,  according  to  his  mother’s  Joyntur.  My  house  in  Wicks  Bishop  and  copy  lands  to

then  living.  My  shipping  to  be  devided  into  two  parts  :  one  part  of  which  I  bequeath  to  my 

two  daughters,  and  the  other  part  equally  to  my  sonnes  William,  Jonathan  and  John.  Wife  to 
give  bond  of  one  thousand  pounds,  in  case  she  marry  again,  to  my  brother  Mr  John  Hammond 
and  to  Mr  Henry  Parkehurst  of  Ipswich.  The  second  day  of  Novr  1667.  Codicil  6th  Novr  1667. 

I  bequeath  one  tenth  part  of  my  whole  estate  to  the  silenced  ministers  :  namely  two  thirds  of  it 

to  the  Presbiterian  ministers  that  need  it  and  one  third  of  it  to  ye  Independents,  begging  their 

Prayers  to  God  for  his  Covenant  blessings  vpon  my  posteritie.  Tricesimo  die  Aprilis  1681  Comiss

Arch.  Suff.  Liber  “  King,”  fo.  20. 

The  Hammonds  of  Ipswich  were  a  race  of  hardy  sea  captains  and  themselves  in  great  part 
owners  of  the  ships  they  sailed  in  and  the  cargoes  they  carried.  They  held  the  Manor  of  Newton 
Hall  in  Swilland  for  several  generations.  Edward  Hammond,  who  died  a  little  after  the  Restoration, 
is  mentioned  with  approval  by  Matthias  Candler,  the  genealogical  Vicar  of  Coddenham.  “  Henry 

Bloomfield,”  he  says,  “  one  of  the  Chiefe  Constables  of  the  Hu  of  Thredling,”  married  to  his 

second  wife,  “  Thomasin  daughter  of  Thomas  Coale  of  Ipswich,  the  relict  of  W“  Peche  a  Mr  of 
a  ship  neere  the  old  Barre  gates  in  Ipswich.  She  had  a  daughter  m.  to  Edward  Hamont 
Mr  of  a  ship  in  Ipswich,  a  pins  man.”  Harl.  MS.  6071,  p.  543.  An  armorial  tombstone  in 

the  churchyard  of  St.  Clement  bears  the  inscription,  “  The  Burying  place  of  Captain  Benjamin 

Hamond  and  Captain  John  Hammond,  sons  of  Edward  Hamond  in  this  parish.”  Then  follow 
names  and  dates.  The  Shield,  Party  per  pale,  displays  a  quatrefoil  between  three  demi-lions 
passant  guardant  ;  and  the  Crest  above,  on  helmet  and  torse,  is  a  wolf’s  head  erased.

Margarett  Father  of  Yoxford  in  the  County  of  Suffolke  widdow,  15  July  1633.  First  I 
bequeath  vnto  Edward  Haraond  of  Westleton  my  nephew  and  to  Sarah  his  wyfe  all  my  messuages 
lands  tenements  &c.  in  UfFord  Melton  and  Bromeswell,  and  to  the  longest  liver  of  them,  and  after 
their  decease  to  William  Hamond  sonne  of  y'  said  Edward  and  Sarah  and  to  his  heires  for  ever; 
and  for  want  of  such  issue  to  John  Hamond  brother  of  the  sayd  William.  Said  William  not  yet 
one  and  twenty  yeares  of  age.  Ynto  sayd  Edward  Hamond  all  my  goods,  ready  money  &c.  Bv 
Indenture  tripartite,  dated  16  April  in  the  tenth  year  of  his  late  maiestye  King  James,  between 
John  Father  my  then  husband  and  me  his  then  wyfe  on  ye  ffirst  pte  and  Henry  Groome,  then 
of  Petistree  and  now  of  Vfford  on  ye  second  pte,  and  William  Glover  late  of  Ash  gent,  and  others 
on  ye  third  pte,  it  was  provided  that  for  consideracohs  therein  named  Henry  Groome  or  Margaret  his 
wife  should  enioy  the  Manor  liowse  called  Otlyes  in  UfFord  where  in  ye  said  Henry  Groome  now 
dwelleth  after  ye  decease  of  y*  aforesaid  John  Father  and  of  me,  and  should  pay  such  sumes  of 

money  as  I  should  will,  not  to  exceed  three  hundred  pounds  in  all.  Now  I  bequeath  unto  Jone  Till 

widdow  fForty  shillinges  :  Ynto  Robert  Geyton  of  Sutton  yeoman  thirty  pounds  :  Vnto  John  Man 
ten  pounds  :  Vnto  Mary  Culham  fine  pounds  &c.  I  appoint  sayd  Edward  Hamond  sole  executor. 
Probat.  29  Oct1'  1633  Edwardo  Hamond.  Arch.  SufFolc.  Original  Wills,  1633,  No.  38. 

The  William  Glover  mentioned  in  this  will  was  brother-in-law  to  Thomas  Hammond  of  Bury 
St.  Edmunds  (see  pp.  252 — 254).  His  son,  William  Glover,  Esq.,  of  Ash  sued  Edward  Hammond, 
the  executor,  for  five  hundred  pounds  which  he  alleged  the  testatrix  had  promised,  so  far  back 
as  1597,  to  leave  him  when  she  died.  ( Glover  c.  Hammond,  Chas.  I,  B  and  A,  GG.  18,  33.) 
She  was  at  that  time  the  widow  of  John  Glover,  his  grandfather.  By  Fine  in  Easter  Term,  1598, 
John  Father,  her  next  husband,  probably  by  way  of  marriage  settlement,  conveyed  his  Manor  of 
Otleys  in  UfFord  to  William  Glover,  her  stepson  ( Suffolk  Fines,  Pasch.,  40  Eliz.),  and  this  sale 

was  confirmed  by  a  similar  Fine  in  1601  ( Suffolk  Fines,  Trinity  Term,  43  Eliz.)  In  1612,  as 

stated  in  the  will,  he  finally  settled  it  upon  Margaret  Groom,  his  wife’s  niece,  who  seems, 
judging  from  her  uncle  Wyberd’s  testamentary  allusions  (see  p.  253),  her  many  marriages,  and 
John  Father’s  liberal  deed  of  gift,  to  have  been  a  very  attractive  woman.  He  made  will  as  John 
Father  of  Pettistree,  yeoman,  on  the  24th  August,  1625,  bequeathing  his  estates  in  Woodbridge, 
UfFord  and  Bromeswell  to  Edward  Hammond,  his  wife’s  nephew,  absolutely.  Probate  was  made 
15  Sept.  1625,  in  the  Registry  of  the  Archdeaconry  of  SufFolk.

three  leopards’  faces  jess  ant  fleurs  de  lys  Or,  and  the  Crest,  On  a  wreath  Or  and  Sable,  a  goat 
Argent,  climbing  a  rock  or  mount  proper,  on  the  top  of  which  grow  three  sprigs  Vert,  flowered 
proper,  apparently  of  the  wild  rose.  The  official  drawing  which  accompanies  the  pedigree  represents 
Gurdon  as  quartering  Sexton,  Argent,  three  sinister  wings  Gules,  and  impaling  Brampton,  Quarterly, 
1  and  4,  Gules,  a  fess  Argent,  in  chief  three  plates,  for  Brampton  ;  2,  Chequy  Or  and  Gules,  a 
bend  Ermine,  for  Basingham  ;  and  3,  Argent,  three  piles  wavy  converging  in  point,  over  all  a  fess 
Argent,  apparently  for  Barton.  This  was,  clearly,  the  authorised  atchievement  of  John  Gurdon,  then 
Lord  of  Assington,  whose  mother  was  coheir  of  Sexton,  and  whose  wife  the  daughter  of  Brampton 
of  Letton  in  Norfolk. 


The  heraldic  MSS.  at  the  British  Museum  and  elsewhere,  although  of  no  real  authority,  give 
some  interesting  variations  of  these  authorised  Arms  and  Quarterings  of  Gurdon.  We  are  told  in 
the  old  family  pedigree  at  Letton  that  the  leopards’  faces  were  originally  argent,  but  that  Robert, 
the  younger  son  of  Sir  Adam  Gurdon,  changed  them  to  gold  to  be  distinguished  from  the  elder 
branch,  then  in  Wiltshire.  The  Arms,  as  tricked  in  Harl.  MS.  1560,  the  best  collection  of  Suffolk 
Visitation  Pedigrees  to  be  found  out  of  the  Heralds’  College,  are  surmounted  by  two  crests  which 
have,  at  one  time  or  another,  been  adopted  by  the  family.  The  one,  which  appears  [upon  the  older 
monuments  at  Assington,  is  a  leopard’s  face,  party  per  pale  Argent  and  Sable,  between  two  wings 
addorsed  counterchanged.  The  other  is  the  Goat  Argent,  horned  Or,  climbing  a  rock  proper,  with 
a  sprig  issuing  from  the  top  Vert.  An  atchievement  follows  which  is  identical  with  that  of  Brampton 
Gurdon  of  Letton  in  the  Norfolk  Visitation  of  1664.  Harl.  MS.  1085.  Beneath  the  second  crest, 
that  with  the  goat,  rock  and  twig,  is  Quarterly  of  Eight : —

The  monuments  at  Assington  are  numerous  and  interesting,  and  one  especially,  of  coloured 
marbles,  erected  in  1648,  is  covered  with  armorial  insignia.  The  Quarterly  of  Eight,  already 
described,  appears  above  the  effigy  of  Brampton  Gurdon.  The  shield  above  that  of  his  wife, 
Elizabeth  Barrett,  as  described  in  the  Davy  MSS.,  is  Quarterly  of  nineteen:  1,  Barrett;  2,  Belhouse  ; 
3,  Braytoft ;  4,  Dyneley ;  5,  Fitzherbert ;  6,  Milo,  Earl  of  Hereford  ;  7,  De  Forte  ;  8,  Cheuduitt ; 
9,  Foscott  ;  10,  Marney  ;  11,  Bruyn  ;  12,  Comyn  ;  13,  Lytton ;  14,  Booth:  15,  Oake  ;  16, 
Weyland  ;  17,  Godmanston  ;  18,  Cavalere  ;  19,  Barrett,  as  before.  The  Crest,  differing  from  those 
depicted  in  the  MSS.,  is  Out  of  a  ducal  coronet  Or,  two  wings  erect  addorsed  Argent.  A  pencil 
drawing  of  this  exceptional  device  is  given  in  Harl.  MS.  1560. 

Other  coats  have  since  been  added.  The  Norfolk  Gordons  for  some  time  quartered  the 
Arms  cf  Dillingham,  whose  heiress  brought  considerable  estates  to  the  family ;  but  in  the  present 
day  they  simply  use  Brampton  quarterly  with  their  own  shield,  in  order  to  distinguish  their 
branch  from  the  Gurdons  of  Suffolk.  The  escutcheon  on  the  monument  of  Nathaniel  Gurdon, 
S.T.P ,  of  Assington,  who  died  in  1696,  has  thirty  quarterings,  many  of  which  are  now  so  much 
defaced  as  to  be  almost  unrecognisable.

John  Gurdon.  I  have  likewise  surrendered  my  coppiehold  lands  and  tenements  holden  of  the

And  fore  as  much  as  business  may  be  hex-eafter  for  my  sickness,  to  the  intent  to  avoid  slanderous

occasion  to  ride  to  Norwich  whereon  I  took  my  journey  thirward  on  horseback  with  my  wyff 
behind  on  Wednesday  fortnight  before  Christmas  in  the  morning  being  a  great  frost  &  at  Sayme 
(Saham)  bridge  a  little  on  this  side  Walton  Market  the  water  was  frozen  &  then  I  caused  my 
horse  to  go  over  the  bridge  &  when  he  was  on  the  middle  bridge  his  foot  slivered  on  the  one 
side  by  reason  that  I  spurred  him  &  so  I  fell  into  the  water  there  with  me  A  myne  wyfe 
wherein  I  had  been  drowned  if  my  wyff  had  not  gotten  up  in  the  water  &  have  taken  me  by 
the  head  &  kepe  it  above  wrater  until  one  Henry  Page  of  Hasshill  did  helpe  me  ought  &  had 
us  both  to  a  house  in  Sayme  &  therefore  I  would  myne  wyff  should  bear  no  charge  nor 

rebuke  for  this  my  sickness  which  came  by  the  mishap  aforesaid  &  none  otherwise.

demonstrations  of  valoire  and  worthiness  diuerslie  distributed  accordinge  to  the  qualities  and  deserte

Thomas  Burrough  of  Wyckliambroke  in  the  Countie  of  Suffolke  gentilinan  hath  vsed  him  selfe  so

George  Burrough,  fourth  and  youngest  son  of  Thomas  Burrough  of  Wickhambrook,  was 
baptized  there  on  the  26th  of  October  1579.  He  entered  Corpus  Christi  College,  Cambridge,  in 
1594,  was  admitted  to  Bishop  Nix’s  Scholarship  in  Trinity  Hall,  26th  May  1597,  and  took  his  degree 
of  LL.B.  in  1600.  He  was  ordained  priest  29th  Sept.  1604,  by  John,  Bishop  of  Norwich,  and  was 
instituted  the  same  year,  on  the  presentation  of  John  Turner,  Gentleman,  to  the  living  of  Pettaugh, 
the  sureties  for  his  First  Fruits  being  his  brother  Thomas  Burrough  of  the  parish  of  St.  Dunstan 
in  the  West,  London,  and  his  cousin  Thomas  Sherman.  In  1621  he  was  permitted  by  dispensation 
of  the  Archbishop  of  Canterbury,  confirmed  under  the  Great  Seal,  14th  March  Jas.  I,  to  hold  the 
adjoining  rectory  of  Gosbeck  together  with  that  of  Pettaugh.  He  retained  Gosbeck,  and  perhaps 
Pettaugh,  during  the  Usurpation,  and  dying  at  the  age  of  seventy-four  was  buried  at  the  latter 
place  on  the  21st  of  February  1653. 

The  Editor  is  indebted  for  most  of  these  particulars  to  the  kindness  of  Dr.  Bensly,  the 
courteous  Registrar  of  the  Bishop  of  Norwich.  They  are  given  in  “  Consignation  Book,”  No.  3,  and 
in  the  Tanner  MSS.,  now  in  the  possession  of  the  see.

( ISitrrottjjIj  of  (England,  1692, 

George  Burrough,  the  American  emigrant  of  the  seventeenth  century,  whose  name  in  his 
adopted  country  was  more  frequently  written  Burrowes,  is  best  known  as  the  chief  victim  of  the 
final  outburst  of  religious  fanaticism  which  tarnishes  the  history  of  the  New  England  settlements. 
His  whole  story  is  tinged  with  adventure.  Son  of  a  Limehouse  merchant  and  grandson  of  the 
puritan  Rector  of  Pettaugh,  it  is  probable  that  his  theological  leanings,  and  much  intercourse  with 
the  old  sea  dogs  of  his  native  place,  led  him  to  cross  the  Atlantic.  He  graduated  at  Harvard 
in  1670.  His  daughter  Rebecca  was  baptized  at  Roxbury  in  1674.  In  1676  we  find  him  preaching 
at  Falmouth,  in  the  province  of  Massachusetts,  with  such  acceptance  that  the  community  granted 
him  two  hundred  acres  for  his  services.  Scarcely  wras  he  thus  settled  when  the  Indians,  thirsting  for 
blood,  swooped  down  upon  the  place  and  massacred  its  inhabitants.  With  such  as  survived  he 
escaped  to  Bang’s  Island  in  the  harbour,  from  whence  he  wrote  the  details  of  the  disaster  which 
were  forwarded  to  the  Governor  and  Council  at  Boston.  In  1680  he  was  ministering  at  Salem, 
where  unhappily  he  made  enemies,  but  had  returned  to  Falmouth  in  1683.  Again  the  Indians  sacked 
the  place,  and  again  he  escaped  with  his  life.  On  the  8th  of  May  1692,  he  was  charged  with 
witchcraft  and  sent  to  prison.  The  official  records  of  his  trial  on  the  3rd  of  August  following  are 
a  sufficient  vindication  of  his  character,  His  indictment,  dated  9th  May  in  the  4th  year  of  William 


BURROUGH  OF  WICKH AMBROOK. 


303 


and  Mary,  King  and  Queen  of  England,  sets  forth  that  George  Bin-rough,  late  of  Falmouth  in  the 
province  of  Massachusetts  Bay,  clerk,  had  used  those  detestable  arts  called  Witchcraft  within  the 
town  of  Salem  against  one  Mary  Walcott  and  others,  she  being  thereby  tortured,  consumed,  wasted 
and  tormented,  against  the  peace  of  our  Sovereign  Lord  and  Lady,  the  said  King  and  Queen. 
Witnesses  confessed  that  he  had  administered  witch  sacraments  at  their  meetings.  Their  testimony, 
such  as  it  was,  was  corroborated  by  circumstantial  evidence.  Burrough  was  a  man  of  extraordinary 
strength  and  activity.  On  one  occasion  he  had  carried  a  cask  of  cyder  unaided  from  a  canoe  to 
the  shore  ;  and  on  another  had  lifted,  and  whirled  around  him,  a  barrel  of  molasses  by  putting  his 
finger  in  the  bunghole  ;  and  on  yet  another  had  held  out  a  gun  of  seven  feet  barrel  with  one 
hand.  Upon  his  urging  that  an  Indian,  who  was  present  on  the  last  occasion,  had  done  the  same,  it 
was  answered  by  his  accusers  that  the  latter  must  have  been  the  Devil,  who,  the  witnesses  swore, 
looks  like  an  Indian.  It  was  said  that  his  house  was  haunted  with  spirits,  that  he  could  tell  what 
his  wives  (for  he  had  been  two  or  three  times  married)  had  been  doing  during  his  absence,  and 
that  he  knew  their  secret  thoughts  Incredible  as  it  may  seem,  he  was  convicted  on  evidence  like 
this.  He  was  hanged  on  the  19th  of  August,  on  the  Gallow’s  Hill  at  Salem.  His  last  prayer  at 
his  funeral,  for  he  was  buried  immediately  afterwards,  was  so  solemn,  pertinent  and  affecting,  that 
Cotton  Mather,  the  fanatical  divine,  who  had  busied  himself  at  his  accusation,  trial  and  execution,  and 
who  had  preached  when  his  last  struggle  had  ended,  was  driven  to  say  that  no  man  could  have 
made  such  a  prayer  unless  the  devil  had  helped  him. 

But  the  witch  finders  had  gone  too  far.  A  man  of  blameless  life,  of  unusual  attainments  and 
of  singular  generosity,  had  been  judicially  murdered,  and  public  opinion  began  to  turn.  One  month 

later,  Giles  Cory,  the  last  that  suffered  from  these  wretched  charges,  refusing  to  plead,  was  pressed 

to  death.  Nineteen  persons  had  been  killed,  professing  their  innocence.  The  gaol  at  Salem  was 
full  of  prisoners.  Accusations  were  bandied  about  in  all  directions,  implicating  members  of  the 
Council  and  even  the  Governor’s  wife,  Lady  Phipps.  It  became  clear  to  all  right  thinking  persons 
that  an  end  must  be  made  to  so  dangerous  a  movement.  At  the  Court  in  January  all  the  prisoners 
were  practically  acquitted.  Mr.  Sewall,  one  of  George  Burrough’s  judges,  at  a  public  fast, 
acknowledged  the  error  he  had  made,  and  desired  to  humble  himself  in  the  sight  of  God.  In  1711, 

the  Government,  confessing  the  wrong  doing,  at  the  instance  of  Charles  Burrough,  one  of  his  sons, 

made  such  restitution  as  was  in  their  power,  and  granted  special  provision  for  his  heirs,  who  still 
held,  it  would  seem,  the  two  hundred  acres  which  had  been  given  him  at  Roxbury. 

George  Burrough  kept  up  his  intercourse  with  his  English  kinsmen  almost  up  to  the  day  of 
his  decease.  He  was  the  chief  heir  to  his  father  in  1C81  and  to  his  uncle,  John  Styles,  in  1685. 
In  1689,  another  uncle,  Charles  Burrough  of  Ipswich,  remembered  him  in  his  will.  He  corresponded, 
mostly  on  business  matters,  with  William  Burrough  of  Staple  Inn,  his  cousin  german,  as  late  as 
1692.  His  affairs  are  referred  to  in  the  Chancery  Proceedings  in  Fere  c.  Burrough,  Mitford  III,  cccxci, 
and  Burrough  c.  Buckland,  Mitford  III,  ccccxii.  He  had  many  children.  By  her  marriage  with  Peter 
Thomas  of  Boston,  liis  daughter  Elizabeth  became  the  ancestress  of  a  numerous  and  distinguished 
progeny,  Isaiah  Thomas,  LL.D.,  who  founded  the  American  Antiquarian  Society,  being  one  of 
her  descendants.  Authorities  : — Savage’s  “  Genealogical  Dictionary,”  Hutchinson’s  “  History  of 
Massachusetts,”  Sewall’s  “  Diary  and  Letter  Book  in  the  Collections  of  the  .Massachusetts  Historical 
Society,”  “New  England  Historical  and  Genealogical  Register,”  Vol.  i,  37,  &c.,  Ac.

Towai’ds  the  middle  of  the  eighteenth  century  the  period  between  death  and  interment, 
which  in  the  time  of  Queen  Elizabeth  and  James  the  First  had  been  but  one  or  twTo  days,  became 
considerably  lengthened,  apparently  from  a  dread  which  had  developed  itself  in  the  public  mind 
of  being  buried  alive.  Indeed  directions  were  not  unfrequently  given  by  will,  as  in  the  present 
instance,  for  a  still  more  protracted  delay ;  some  testators  even  insisting  that  their  body  should 
be  kept  an  entire  fortnight  in  an  open  coffin  before  it  was  finally  committed  to  the  ground.

neices  Margaret  Burrough  and  Elizabeth  Burrough.  Said  Nathaniel  Highmore  and  Thomas  Sibthorpe 
to  sell  my  messuage  at  Guildford.  To  John  Ewart  of  Brampton  in  the  county  of  Cumberland 
the  sum  of  fforty  pounds,  as  a  token  of  my  grateful  remembrance  of  the  kindness  he  has  shewn 
to  myself,  nephews  and  neices.  To  my  servant  James  Blanch  the  sum  of  ffive  hundred  pounds. 
I  do  direct  that  the  clear  residue  of  my  personal  estate  shall  be  divided  into  five  equal  parts, 
and  executors  shall  pay  one  part  to  Mary  Strong,  one  to  John  Burrough,  one  to  Charles  Burrough, 
one  to  Margaret  Burrough  and  the  remaining  part  to  Elizabeth  Burrough.  And  I  do  appoint 

the  said  Nathaniel  Highmore  and  Thomas  Sibthorpe  to  be  executors.  1  do  declare  this  only  to 
be  my  last  will  this  seventh  day  of  December  1772. 

By  Codicil  dated  7  Novr  1775  the  testator  devised  his  messuage  at  Guildford  to  James 
Blanch  his  servant  and  his  heirs  for  ever.  By  another  Codicil,  7th  June  1776,  he  left  to  the 
said  James  Blanch  all  his  printed  books,  his  bureaus,  salts,  drinking  glasses,  china,  table  clock 
made  by  Tho.  Tompion,  his  ffurniture  Ac.  Ac.  ;  to  the  wife  of  Mr  Anthony  Highmore  and  the 
longest  liver  of  her  daughters,  his  gold  repeating  watch;  to  Anthony  Highmore  junior  his  small 
gold  watch  with  the  gold  chain  and  seals  thereunto  belonging. 

This  will  was  proved,  with  Codicils,  the  seventh  day  of  November  1780  by  the  oaths  of 

the  executors.  P.C.C.  504  Collins.

In  most  humble  wise  complayning  sheweth  Pliillipp  Forthe  of  Hadleighe  in  the  Countie  of 
Suff.  gentleman,  that  Wittm  Forthe  late  of  Hadleighe,  Esquier,  fatlier  vnto  yor  Orator,  was  in 
his  life  tyme  seased  of  oue  capital  messuage  &  threeskore  acres  of  land  in  Hadleigh  aforesaid 

and  of  divers  other  lands  in  Hadleighe,  Reydon,  Hundlesham  and  Aldham,  to  the  yerely  valewe 
of  one  hundred  pounds.  And  soe  seased  did,  abowte  the  eighteenth  yere  of  the  Queues  Matie 
that  nowe  is,  take  to  wyfe  Dorothe  Harvey,  and  for  her  joynture  did  convey  said  lands  and 
tenements  vnto  John  Kene  late  of  Starston  in  the  Countie  of  Norff.  gent,  and  Edward  Bacon  of

Unmindful  of  the  parish  registers  and  the  inscription  in  Hadleigh  Church,  the  pedigree  on 
page  119  of  the  present  volume,  following  too  closely  Hark  MS.  1560,  makes  the  younger  sons 
of  William  Forth  to  be  the  children  of  a  second  wife,  the  daughter  of  .  .  .  Kene.  It  is  clear, 
however,  as  well  from  the  inscription  and  registers  referred  to  as  from  the  Chancery  Proceedings 
just  recited  and  the  Kene-Harvey  pedigree  in  Hark  MS.  1552,  that  Dorothy  Harvey  was  the 
mother,  and  Joan  Kene  the  grandmother,  of  the  sons  in  question,  in  common  with  their  brothers 
and  their  sister.

James  Tillie  of  Pentillie  Castle  in  Cornwall,  complainant.  John  Forth  Esqr,  heretofore 
Alderman  of  London,  had  large  brewhouses  at  Kingston  on  Thames  and  Taunton  co.  Somerset 
and  sugar  works  in  Middlesex  and  iron- works  in  Worcestershire  and  was  a  Farmer  of  the  Excise 
and  of  the  Kings  Revenues  in  Ireland.  He  became  indebted  to  His  Majesty  fifty  thousand 
pounds  and  mortgaged  his  property.  He  died  intestate  in  Decr  1676,  leaving  issue  by  Albinia 
his  relict,  a  daughter  of  Sir  Henry  Vane,  Henry  Forth  an  infant  of  very  tender  years,  and  by 
a  former  wife  Elizabeth  Forth  and  Martha  Forth  then  under  age.  Albinia  in  forlorn  condition 
sought  assistance  of  your  Orator,  who  afterwards  married  -.  .  .  Vane  one  of  her  sisters,  and 
your  Orator  helped  them  all.  Matthew  Meade  of  London,  clerk,  and  Dame  Frances  Vane,  mother 
of  said  Albinia,  were  parties  to  trusts.  Albinia  died  in  August  or  September,  1679.  Thomas 
Hillersden  Esqr  had  married  Anne,  eldest  sister  of  the  whole  blood  to  Elizabeth  and  Martha,  and 
Joseph  Dawson,  Alderman  of  London,  deceased,  married  one  other  sister.  Christopher  Vane  Esqr, 
now  Christopher  Lord  Bernard  was  himself  a  creditor  of  John  Forth,  who  was  greatly  involved. 
Your  Orator  preserved  some  houses  at  Stroud  Green  Ac.  for  Henry  Forth  the  son  who  was  under 
his  care.  Elizabeth  Forth  abovenamed  married  Nicholas  Wildbore  and  Martha  Forth  one  Hillersden 
of  Devonshire.  Henry  Forth  came  of  age  and,  influenced  by  some  of  his  great  relations,  brought 
actions  at  law  against  your  Orator.  Reynardson  I.  and  II,  475-80.

Appleton  of  WaltirngfieltL 


Armorial  Hearings. 

The  Arms  of  Appleton  of  Waldingfield,  at  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1577,  were  Argent,  a  fess 
Sable,  between  three  apples  Gules,  stalked  and  leaved  Vert.  The  Crest,  an  elephant’s  head  Sable, 

eared  and  tusked  Or,  wreathed  round  the  trunk  a  snake  entering  the  mouth  Vert.  The  same 

Arms  and  Crest  were  allowed  at  the  Visitation  of  1664,  with  a  shield  of  pretence,  for  More  of 
Wiggenhall  St.  Germain,  Sable,  a  swan  with  wings  expanded  Argent,  beaked  and  legged  Or, 
within  a  border  engrailed.  A  separate  escutcheon  at  the  side  of  the  tricking  in  Harl.  MS.  10S5 
has  More  quartering  Ermine  a  spear’s  head  embrued  with  blood  proper. 

On  the  brass  of  Mary  Appleton,  1526,  in  the  church  of  Waldingfield  Magna,  her  figure  is 
surmounted  by  an  achievement  in  which  Appleton  quarters  Crane,  Argent,  a  fess  between  three 
crosses  crosslet  fitchee  Gules,  and  impales  Mountney,  Azure,  a  bend  between  six  martlets  Or. 

Some  heraldic  collections  of  the  seventeenth  century,  as,  for  example,  Harl.  MSS.  1196 
and  1560 ,  represent  Appleton’s  coat  as  Quarterly  of  twelve  :  1,  Appleton;  2,  Crane;  3,  Mollington, 

Or,  a  fess  between  two  chevrons  Azure  ;  4,  Carbonell,  Gules,  a  cross  Argent,  within  a  border 

engrailed  Or ;  5,  Butler,  Argent,  three  covered  cups  in  bend  Sable,  cotised  Gules  ;  6,  Sexton  ; 
7,  Mountney  ;  8,  Isack,  Sable,  a  bend  Or,  in  sinister  chief  a  leopard’s  face  of  the  second ; 
9,  Condy,  “  Vice-admirall  to  the  Kynge,”  Barry  wavy  Argent  and  Azure,  three  anchors  Or  (the 
MSS.  differ  as  to  the  number  of  bars  and  of  anchors);  10,  Tuke,  per  chevron  Argent  and  Sable, 
three  cranes’  heads  erased  counterchanged  ;  11,  Hawte,  Or,  a  cross  engrailed  Gules  ;  12,  Wheathill, 
per  fess  Azure  and  Or,  a  pale  counterchanged,  three  lions  rampant  of  the  second.  Crest,  out  of 
a  ducal  coronet  Or,  three  pine  apples  Vert,  the  tops  purfled  of  the  first.  Motto,  “  Difficilis 
sed  fructuosa.” 

It  should  be  observed  that  these  MSS.  have  no  official  authority,  that  the  crest  they 
depict  is  not  that  of  the  Suffolk  Visitations,  and  that  some  at  least  of  the  numerous  quarterings 
attributed  to  Appleton  have  been  assumed  upon  evidence  which  is  exceedingly  doubtful. 

An  excellent  account  of  the  Waldingfield  family  will  be  found  in  the  “Memorial  of  Samuel 
Appleton  of  Ipswich,  Massachusetts,”  by  Isaac  Appleton  Jewett.  It  gives  in  full  the  pedigrees 
of  Appleton  and  Isaaclc  of  Kent  from  Harl.  MS.  1196,  together  with  engravings,  including  the 
brass  of  Mary  Appleton,  and  with  transcripts  of  family  documents,  such  as  the  most  genealogical 
will  of  liobert  Byece,  1637,  and  the  ancient  Appleton  inscriptions  at  Waldingfield,  as  copied  by 
Weever.  On  the  other  hand,  the  Appleton  Pedigree  and  Arms  from  the  Visitation  of  1577  and 
from  Harl.  MS.  1560,  will  be  found  in  that  useful  work,  “The  Visitations  of  Suffolk,”  edited  by 
Walter  C.  Metcalfe,  F.S.A.

brother  in  law  John  Butler  Esquire  and  Ambrose  Butler  gent.,  of  the  Inner  Temple  London,  and 
my  sonne  Robert  Cradocke  Cittizen  and  Vintner  of  London,  to  doe  all  lawful  and  reasonable 
things  in  order  to  this  sale.  I  and  my  brother  Fairbeard  and  his  wife  did  agree  with  Mr  Marriott 
for  the  sale  of  each  of  our  third  parts  but  there  were  differences  touching  the  same.  My 
executors  shall  put  out  two  hundred  pounds  for  the  vse  of  my  two  grandchildren,  daughters  of 
Dorothy  Goodbody  deceased,  and  I  do  dispose  of  two  hundred  pounds  unto  my  daughter  Anne 
Garway.  My  sonne  in  lawe  John  Garway  is  bound  for  my  sonne  Robert  Cradocke.  I  doe  make 
my  loveing  freinds  John  Garway  of  London  Vintner  and  Baron  Turner  of  London  Goldsmith, 
Executors.  All  other  my  estate  I  give  vnto  my  sone  Robert  Craddock.  Probatum  7  Martij  1667 
Juramentis  executorum.  P.C.C.  35  Carr.

Weever’s  “  Funeral  Monuments,”  p.  759. 

The  brief  but  authentic  pedigree  of  Appleton  of  Waldingfield,  taken  by  Cooke,  Clareucieux, 
at  the  Suffolk  Visitation  in  1577,  begins  with  the  marriage  of  William  Appleton  with  Rose  Sexton. 

But  Harl.  MSS.  1560  and  1196  add,  upon  what  authority  we  know  not,  a  number  of  earlier 

descents.  John  Appleton  of  Waldingfield  Magna,  1416,  they  say,  had  issue  John  Appleton  of 
Waldingfield  Magna,  1459,  and  he  in  his  turn  had  two  sons,  Thomas,  who  died  in  1467,  and 
John,  who  died  in  1483 — the  latter  being  father,  by  Margaret  his  wife,  of  Thomas  Appleton,  who 
married  Margaret  Crane.  These  MSS.,  helpful  as  they  are,  abound  with  statements  which  are  not 
supported  by  evidences.  Together  with  the  Appleton  genealogies  compiled  by  Candler  and  Blois  in 
the  time  of  the  Usurpation,  they  form  the  basis  of  the  pedigree  which  appears  on  the  next  page.

Like  most  of  the  pedigrees  in  the  Harleian  MSS.,  that  of  Appleton  above  given  cannot  be  relied  upon  for  exactitude  of 
statement  in  all  its  details.  Margery  Crane,  the  wife  of  Thomas  Appleton,  was  not  the  daughter,  but  the  sister  of  the  Robert  Crane 
who  married  Anne  Ogard,  and  is  indeed  so  described  by  him  in  his  will,  now  in  the  custody  of  the  Dean  and  Chapter  of  Canterbury. 
We  learn  alike  from  his  Inquisition  post  mortem  and  from  the  will  of  Dame  Anne  Arundel,  his  relict,  that  he  died  without 
surviving  issue  and  that  Robert  Crane,  his  brother’s  son,  was  his  heir.  Alice  Spring,  again,  the  second  wife  of  Thomas  Spring 
of  Lavenham,  was  the  daughter  of  one  King  of  Boxford.  Margery  Spring  (not  Alice  as  stated  on  p.  73),  the  first  wife,  was 
sister  and  executrix  of  Thomas  Appleton.  To  this  day  it  is  not  quite  certain  whether  William  Appleton,  who  married  Rose  Sexton 
and  Edward  Appleton,  his  brother,  were  not  the  nephews  rather  than  the  sons  of  Robert  Appleton  and  Mary  Mounteney,  who 
left  no  wills,  and  died  unnoticed  by  the  escheators  of  their  day.

the  fourth  yeare  of  my  age  above  threescore 
Revokeing  all  the  wills  I  made  before 
make  this  my  last.  And  First  I  doe  implore 
Allmighty  God,  into  his  hands  to  take 
my  soule  which  not  alone  himselfe  did  make 
But  did  redeeme  it  with  the  pretious  bloode 
of  his  Deare  sonne ;  that  tytle  still  holds  good. 

I  next  bequeath  my  body  to  the  dust 

From  whence  it  Came,  which  is  no  more  than  just. 

Desireing  yet  that  it  bee  laid  close  by 
my  eldest  daughter  though  I  say  not  why, 

And  leave  my  Grandchild  Martha  (but  her  due) 

my  Lands  and  all  my  Chattells  save  a  fewe 

you  shall  hereafter  in  this  schedule  finde 

to  pyetye  or  Charitye  designed, 

wliome  I  my  Sole  Executrix  invest

And  then  I  shall  not  Care  how  sooue  I  dye

There’s  not  a  man  of  them  but  is  so  just

“  Dr.  Edward  H.  Williams  has  been  prominently  identified  with  educational  matters  in  the  United  States,  having  erected 
and  equipped  buildings  for  teaching  pure  and  applied  science  at  Carleton  College  (in  memory  of  his  son  William),  and  at  the 
University  of  Vermont  (in  memory  of  his  wife),  and  has  given  largely  to  the  University  of  Pennsylvania  and  other  institutions.” 

*  Gershom  Palmer  was  descended  from  George  Denison  of  Stouington,  Connecticut,  who  returned  to  Europe  for  a  time,  serving 
as  Captain  under  Oliver  Cromwell,  both  in  England  and  Ireland.  Coming  back  to  America,  he  was  placed  second  in  command 
of  the  colonial  troops,  whom  he  headed  in  the  war  which  destroyed  the  Narragansett  nation,  taking  prisoner  their  chief 
Miantonomo.  He  died  at  Hartford,  during  a  session  of  the  General  Court,  of  which  he  was  for  many  years  a  member.

Armorial  Umrngs. 

The  Arms  allowed  at  the  Visitation  of  London  in  1664  to  “John  Doget,  mchant,”  descended 
from  “  Grotten  in  Suff:  ”  were  Gules,  two  greyhounds  salient  combatant,  Or,  collared  Argent.  The 
crest  was  an  unicorn’s  head,  Ermine,  maned  Or,  horned  Argent.  Earl.  MS.  1086.  The  shield 
is  a  slight  variant  of  that  of  Doggett  of  Honingham  and  Shernbourn  in  Norfolk,  in  which  the 
greyhounds  are  collared  Sable.  But  the  crest  of  the  latter  family  is  altogether  distinct — a  lion’s 
head  erased,  Or,  gorged  with  a  mural  coronet,  Sable.  Harl.  MS.  1552.  These  insignia,  together 
■with  others  borne  by  various  families  of  the  name,  form  the  frontispiece  of  the  “  History  of  the 
Doggett — Daggett  Family,”  by  Samuel  Bradlee  Doggett,  one  of  those  excellent  genealogies  for 
which  the  Americans  are  famous,  the  result  of  prolonged  and  often  costly  research,  alike  amongst 
the  ancient  records  of  this  country  and  the  more  modern  registries  on  the  other  side  of  the 
Atlantic.  This  work,  for  which  the  Editor  is  indebted  for  much  useful  information,  abounds  with 
illustrations,  the  views  of  Groton  and  Boxford  Churches  being  exceptionally  clear  and  artistic.

Kingston,  Jamaica,  8th  July  1703.  Dear  Brother.  It  is  now  about  a  week  since  I  received 
two  letters  from  you,  the  one  da.ted  in  November  the  other  in  January,  in  which  I  had  one 

inclosed  from  sister  de  Bary.  I  am  just  crawld  out  of  a  very  severe  ffeaver,  and  after  that 

ffeaver  an  Ague,  which  by  the  help  of  God  and  the  Jesuits  Bark  is  gone,  but  shall  be  some 

time  before  I  recover  my  strength.  About  three  weekes  since  had  a  letter  from  your  wife 

who  has  been  sick  of  a  ffeaver  but  recovered.  (Here  follows  a  passage  in  cypher).  lie  serve  her 
in  everything  lyes  in  my  power.  And  now  I  must  tell  you  that  on  the  fourth  instant  by  the 
packett  Boat  I  received  a  letter  from  my  Brother  Otgher  with  an  account  of  my  Mother’s  death. 
When  I  consider  how  little  advantage  she  had  of  liveing  it  is  my  opinion  she  is  in  the  happier 
state  now.  I  here  send  you  a  coppy  of  part  of  the  letter  that  my  brother  Otgher  sent  me.  Pray 
take  noe  notice  of  haveing  received  any  letter  from  me — it  will  doe  me  a  diskiudness. 

“  She  has  made  me  (he  writes)  her  sole  executrix,  but  your  brother  John  has  thought  fitt  to 
enter  a  Caveat  against  my  Administring,  and  will  perhaps  make  me  spend  some  money  which  would 
have  done  you  and  others  good.  There  will  be  nothing  comeing  to  him,  and  indeed  his  circumstances 
is  very  bad.  He  hath  done  very  ill  to  come  from  his  wife  and  children  at  Carolina  to  serve  the 
Coll :  who  is  but  in  bad  circumstances  himself.  He  thinketh  to  frighten  me  by  his  rough  course, 
and  force  me  to  comply  with  him,  but  he  hath  mistaken  his  man.  Your  mother’s  estate  is  already 
by  losses  and  by  her  weakness  greatly  reduced — which  is  none  of  my  fault.  She  has  left  you  201 
for  mourning  and  -}  of  the  Residue,  you  allowing  3601  out  of  it  which  she  formerly  advanced  you. 
I  doubt  not  something  will  be  comeing  to  you  but  can  make  you  noe  dividend  till  I  have  done 
with  your  brother.  Your  brother  is  to  pay  6201  which  he  had  advanced  to  him  before  he  is  to 
have  his  }  of  the  estate.  I  am  sure  he  will  be  a  debtor  to  the  estate  and,  if  he  crosse  me,  can 
charge  him  with  more.  I  heare  he  lodgeth  in  the  Fleet,  where  he  will  have  noe  good  Councell 
given  him.  But  I  value  not  the  worst  he  can  doe.”

The  Baggs  just  goeing  so  cannot  inlarge.  Since  we  are  all  mortall,  and  a  little  I  have  to

■will  and  leave  you  all  I  can  lay  claime  to.  My  service  to  honest  Tony,  and  all  friends  who  ask 
after  (me).  I  am  in  hast,  dear  Jack,  your  truely  loving  brother,  Ben.  Dogett.  To  Mr  John  Doggett.

Elizabeth  Dogett  of  College  Hill  in  the  City  of  London,  Spinster,  9  June  1765.  Unto 
my  very  worthy  Friend  Alexander  Broughton  of  South  Carolina,  Esquire,  one  Gold  Ring  as  a

Armorial  Scarings. 

The  Arms,  which  accompany  the  earlier  pedigrees  of  Drury,  as  for  example  in  Harl.  MS. 
891,  are  Quarterly,  1  and  4,  Drury ;  2,  Freysell  ;  3,  Saxham.  Later  on,  as  the  heiresses  they 
married  added  their  shields  to  the  family  escutcheon,  the  Drury  quarterings  became  considerably 
augmented.  The  Drurys  of  Sussex,  who  claimed  descent  from  Thomas  Drury  of  Rougham,  1473, 
and  Catherine  Whitwell,  his  wife,  bore  Quarterly  of  Eight ;  1  and  8,  Drury ;  2,  Saxham  ;  3, 
Freysell  ;  4,  Gedding ;  5,  Naunton  ;  6,  Aspall ;  and  7,  Whitwell.  The  Arms  upon  the  monument 
in  Rougham  chancel  to  the  memory  of  Sir  Robert  Drury,  who  died  early  in  the  reign  of  Charles 
the  First,  agree  substantially  with  those  allowed  to  Robert  Drury  of  Tendring,  a  descendant  of 

the  Rougham  family,  at  the  Essex  Visitation  of  1664,  a  tricking  of  which  appears  in  Harl.  MS. 

1085,  and  in  the  corresponding  MS.  at  the  College  of  Arms.  (See  the  edition  of  Bysshe’s 
Visitation  of  that  County,  edited  by  Dr.  J.  J.  Howard,  Maltravers  Herald.)  They  are  as  follows  : — 

Arms. — Quarterly  of  10;  a  mullet  for  difference: — 

1,  Drury,  Argent,  on  a  chief  Vert,  two  mullets  Or,  pierced  Gules. 

2,  Saxham,  Argent,  six  cross  crosslets  fitchee  Gules,  3,  2  and  1,  a  chief  dancettee  Azure. 

3,  Freysell,  Sable,  six  cinquefoils  Argent,  3,  2  and  1. 

4,  Gedding,  Chequy,  Argent  and  Gules,  on  a  fess  Azure,  three  round  buckles  Or,  tongues 

fessways  to  the  dexter  side. 

5,  Naunton,  Sable,  three  martlets  Argent. 

6,  Aspale,  Azure,  three  chevronels  Or. 

7,  Whitwell,  Gules,  a  fess  chequy  Argent  and  Sable,  between  three  pairs  of  annulets 

interlaced  Or. 

8,  Liston,  Vert,  ten  bezants,  3,  3,  3  and  1. 

9,  Carbonell,  Gules,  a  cross  Argent  within  a  bordure  engrailed  Or. 

10,  Bovill,  Quarterly,  Or  and  Sable. 

Crest. — A  greyhound  courant  Argent,  collared  and  ringed  Or.  Below  this  monument  is 
another  representing  a  woman  in  a  winding  sheet,  with  Drury  impaling  Sable,  two  bars  embattled 

and  counter-embattled  Argent,  and  in  chief  three  plates,  apparently  for  Barnes  of  Cambridgeshire. 

As  is  well-known  to  genealogists,  the  Drurys  of  Hawstead,  who  descend  from  a  younger  brother 
of  the  Drurys  of  Rougham,  added  a  Tau  cross  to  the  mullets  on  the  chief  in  the  family  arms, 
a  fact  which  has  given  rise  to  many  ingenious  conjectures.  See  “  East  Anglian  Notes  and 
Queries,”  1858,  &c.,  Vol.  I,  pp.  12,  18,  and  Vol,  III.,  p.  214. 

The  descents  which  follow  are  based  for  the  most  part  upon  the  fine  Drury  pedigrees,  now 
in  the  possession  of  Sir  Hereward  Wake  and  of  F.  S.  E.  Drury,  Esq.,  which  were  compiled  in 
1612  by  Thomas  Drury  of  Rougham,  and  used  by  Sir  John  Cullum  in  the  preparation  of  his 
“  History  of  Hawstead.”  Valuable  additions  have  been  made  from  the  Drury  pedigrees  in 
Add.  MS.  5523,  which  are  annotated  by  Le  Neve,  and  in  Harl.  MS.  6071,  which  were  written 
by  Matthias  Candler,  a  Suffolk  contemporary  of  many  of  the  later  members  of  the  family.

I  Jane  Drury  doe  make  my  last  will  in  manner  following.  First  I  give  my  soule  to  god  and  my  bodie  to  be 
buried  in  the  Church  of  Pulborough.  Vnto  my  nephew  Francis  Drury,  the  sonne  of  my  brother  William,  the  some 
of  one  thousand  pounds,  And  if  he  shall  die  before  hee  shall  come  to  the  age  of  xxi  yeares,  it  shall  be  paid  to  the 
next  heire  of  my  said  brother.  The  vse  of  the  said  some  slialbe  imploied  towards  the  edvcac’on  of  my  said  nephew. 

I  give  to  my  loving  Aunte,  the  Lady  Apsley,  fiftie  pounds  to  buie  her  a  Juell.  To  my  Cosin,  Peter  Apsley,  fortie 

pounds  to  buie  him  a  ringe.  To  my  coseu,  Joyce  Blount,  tenn  poundes  to  buie  her  a  ringe.  To  my  cosen  Lucy 

Apsley  a  pearle  chaine  of  my  owne.  I  give  to  my  foure  brothers  v’  a  peece.  I  will  that  my  cosen,  John  Apsley, 

and  my  cosen  Laurence  Pay,  shall  have  the  putting  out  of  the  thousand  pounds  given  to  my  nephew  Francis 
Drury,  till  hee  come  to  the  age  of  one  and  twenty,  and  in  the  meauetime  shall  take  care  for  his  educac’on  and 
bringing  vpp.  And  also  shall  have  the  disposing  of  the  fiftie  poundes  wcl1  I  give  to  my  goddaughter  aud  ueeee 
Susanna  Drury,  my  brother  William’s  daughter.  To  my  said  cosen,  John  Apsley,  for  his  paines  xx'.  To  my  cosen 
Laurence  Pay,  my  silver  bason  and  x1  to  buie  an  ewer  to  it.  To  the  poore  people  of  Pulborough  x1.  To  my 
godson  George  Boord  100’.  The  rest  of  my  goodes  I  give  to  my  deere  sister  Mrs  Mary  Boord  whom  I  make, 
together  with  her  husband  Mr  Harbert  Boord,  my  sole  and  whole  executors.  The  last  day  of  March,  1629. 
Probatum  sexto  die  Octobris,  1629.  Juramento  Marie  Boord  et  Harberti  Boord.  P.C.C.  86  Ridley. 

*  John  Drury  of  Pulborough,  son  of  Humphrey  of  Salop,  took  his  degree  of  B.C.L.  Oxford,  1578,  and  of  D.C.L., 
17  March  1584-5.  He  was  appointed  Canon  of  Chichester,  1582,  Rector  of  Pulborough,  1589,  Rector  of  Witney, 
Oxon,  and  Archdeacon  of  Oxford,  1592.  His  Arms  and  quarterings,  as  indicated  on  page  345,  were  those  of  Drury  of 
Rougham,  with  a  crescent  for  difference.  His  Crest  was  a  greyhound  courant  Sable,  collared  Or.  Harl.  MS.  1562.

The  Arms,  Quarterings,  and  Crest  allowed  to  Drury  of  Tendring  at  the  Essex  Visitation  of  1664  were  those  of  Drury  of 
Rougham  (see  page  345),  with  a  mullet  for  difference.

JUntorial  Searings. 

The  Arms  of  Drury,  as  depicted  upon  the  monuments  in  Hawstead  chancel  to  Sir  Robert 
Drury,  1615,  and  to  Elizabeth  Drury  his  daughter,  1610,  and  upon  the  tomb  of  his  sister,  Lady 
Wray,  at  Ashby  in  Lincolnshire,  are,  in  effect,  Quarterly  of  13  : — 

1,  Drury,  Argent,  on  a  chief  Vert,  a  cross  Tau  between  two  mullets  pierced  Or. 

2,  Saxham,  Argent,  six  cross  crosslets  fitchee  Gules,  3,  2  and  1,  a  chief  dancettee  Azure. 

3,  Freysell,  Sable,  six  cinquefoils  Argent,  3,  2  and  1. 

4,  Gedding,  Chequy,  Argent  and  Gules,  on  a  fess  Azure,  three  round  buckles  Or. 

5,  Sotehill,  Gules,  an  eagle  displayed  Argent. 

6,  Plompton,  Azure,  three  fusils  in  fess  Or,  each  charged  with  an  escallop  Gules. 

7,  Vilers,  Azure,  a  fess  Or,  between  six  lions  rampant  Argent. 

8,  Murdac,  Bendy  of  10,  Argent  and  Azure. 

9,  Boyville,  Gules,  a  fess  Or,  between  three  saltires  couped  Argent. 

10,  Endesor,  Argent,  a  fess  between  three  horse-shoes  Gules. 

11,  Beaufils,  Gules,  three  fusils  in  fess  barry  wavy  Argent  and  Azure. 

12,  Foljambe,  Sable,  a  bend  between  six  escallops  Or. 

13,  Poynings,  Barry  Or  and  Vert,  a  bend  Gules. 

Quarterings  Nos.  5  to  13,  which  were  brought  in  by  the  Sotehill  marriage,  occur  in  a 
pedigree  in  Philpotts’  “  Suffolk  ”  at  the  College  of  Arms.  They  are  given  on  the  shield  of  Elizabeth 
Sotehill,  as  impaled  with  those  of  her  husband,  Sir  William  Drury,  on  his  brass  in  Hawstead 
church,  1557,  figured  by  Gage.  The  Crest  of  Drury  of  H awstead,  like  that  of  Drury  of  Rougham, 
is  a  greyhound  courant  Argent,  collared  and  ringed  Or.  A  crescent  is  sometimes  added  for 
difference. 

The  Suffolk  historians,  Cullum  in  his  “  History  of  Hawstead,”  and  Gage  in  his  “  History  of 
Thingoe,”  have  devoted  many  pages  to  their  most  interesting  memoirs  of  the  Druries.  The  latter 
has  given  us,  almost  in  extenso,  the  wills  of  five  members  of  the  Hawstead  house ;  those,  namely, 
of  Nicholas  Drury  of  Bury,  1454;  Elizabeth,  wife  of  Henry  Drury,  1475;  Roger  Drury,  1493 
Sir  Robert  Drury,  1532 ;  and  Sir  William  Drury,  1557.  That  of  Dame  Anne  Drury  of  Hardwick, 
1621,  widow  of  Sir  Robert,  will  be  found  in  “Bury  Wills  and  Inventories,”  edited  for  the  Camden 
Society  by  that  excellent  antiquary  the  late  Samuel  Tymms,  F.S.A.

Proved  at  London  14th  Novr,  1606,  by  Sir  William  Cecill,  Lord  Burghley,  and  Sir  William 
Wraye,  the  Executors.  P.C.C.  81  Stafford. 

This  lady,  who  was  sister  to  the  last  Sir  Robert  Drury  of  Hawstead,  went  a  hunting 
whilst  on  a  visit  to  Lady  Wray  at  Glentworth  in  Lincolnshire.  Being  no  horsewoman  they 
fastened  her  to  her  saddle  with  straps  that  she  might  not  be  dismounted.  The  animal  became 
restive  and  ran  away,  galloping  furiously  across  the  country.  Her  head  dashed  against  the  branches 
of  a  tree,  and  the  injuries  were  fatal.  She  had  time,  it  would  seem,  to  make  this  will  before 

she  died.  She  was  buried  in  Ashby  church,  hard  by,  where  a  splendid  monument  was  erected 

to  her  memory.  Her  effigy  reclines  on  a  tomb  supported  by  two  greyhounds  segant  collared. 
“  Unhappy  only  in  her  death,”  says  the  Latin  inscription,  “  she  burst  the  portals  on  the  feast 
day  of  St.  Michael,  1606,  and  joined  the  choirs  of  the  blessed,  having  numbered  but  two  and 
twenty  years.”  “Gentleman’s  Magazine,”  1831,  part  2,  p.  594.

by  the  merritts  and  passion  of  his  Son  Jesus  Christ,  the  love  of  my  life  and  the  life  of  my  soule, 
myne  onely  Savior  and  Redeemer.  My  mynde  is  that  my  Bodye  be  buried  in  decent  and  Christian 
manner  wthout  pompe,  in  the  Church  of  the  parrish  where  it  shall  please  God  to  call  me,  myne

all  vnto  Sr  Henry  Drury  of  Hudgley,  vntill  my  sisters,  and  those  challenging  by  their  right, 
have  given  to  Sr  Henry  Drury  and  to  Sr  Drew  Drury  assurance  of  Drury  house  and  Snarshill 
and  those  landes  in  Norfolke,  that  their  may  be  noe  contention.  I  will  that  Sr  Henry  Drury  or 
his  lieire  ioyned  w*  my  wife  shall  receave  the  profits  of  my  landes  in  Suffolke  for  the  raysinge 
of  five  thowsand  pound  to  be  payed  vnto  a  noble  person  whoe  I  have  bin  iustly  bound  to  make 
that  acknowledgment  for  many  fauoures  and  assistances  in  my  necessity.  To  my  honest  Tutor, 
Mr  Brabon,  parson  of  Whepsteed,  Twenty  pounds  by  yeare,  to  be  levyed  out  of  my  Mannor  of 

Whepsteed  all  the  tyme  of  his  life.  I  doe  make  my  Executoi's  my  loveinge  wife,  Sr  Henry 

Drury  of  Hudgley  and  my  Tutor  Mr  Brabon  and  my  good  honest  friend  Mr  Bamont  of  Cheuing- 
ton,  to  whome  a  peece  of  plate  of  Twenty  pounds  for  a  legacy.  And  I  wish  the  Aimes  house 
may  be  removed  to  Sparrowes  tuft  hard  by  the  Church  at  Hawsteed.  In  testimony  that  this  is 
my  last  will,  which  I  hope  nobody  will  be  so  unloving  unto  me  as  to  endeavour  to  break  it, 
I  have  sett  to  my  hand  and  seale  this  xxvth  of  Aprill  1614  to  both  sides  of  this  paper.  R.  Drury. 
If  it  should  please  God  to  call  that  party  before  me  to  whome  I  have  bequeathed  the  five 
Thowsand  pounde  I  will  that  it  should  be  devided  equally  betweene  my  Sisters. 

A  Codicill  or  parte  of  the  Will  of  the  right  worth  Sr  Robert  Drury,  Knight,  made  the 
second  day  of  Aprill  1615.  Whereas  by  my  will  bearinge  date  the  five  and  twenty  of  Aprill 
1614  I  did  give  vnto  a  noble  personage  five  thowsand  poundes,  my  will  is  now  to  Revoke  that 
legacy,  and  hereby  I  doe  give  vnto  the  same  person  onely  the  some  of  two  thowsand  and  fiue 
hundred  pounds.  And  I  doe  further  giue  unto  my  most  worthy  lady  and  loveinge  wife  two 
thowsand  pounds,  to  be  raysed  out  of  the  revennewes  of  my  said  Mannors  and  lands.  And  alsoe 
I  doe  give  vnto  my  wife  my  Mannor  or  farm  called  Hencote  ferme  near  vnto  Bury  St.  Edmunds 
for  terme  of  her  life,  besides  her  Thirds  and  Dower.  If  any  one  of  my  sisters,  shall  challenge 
any  right  in  those  landes  which  I  have  bequeathed  vnto  my  wife,  then  the  said  my  wife  shall 
enter  into  my  Mannors  of  Hawsteed,  Whepsteed,  Brockley,  Chedber  and  Reed  vntill  she  shall  haue 
peaceable  possession  of  those  landes  wch  I  have  given  her.  Alsoe  I  doe  furder  give  by  this 
Codicill  to  my  beloved  Tewtor,  Mr  Brabon,  one  hundred  poundes  to  buy  him  bookes  wth  all.  I 
doeth  give  vnto  my  good  friend  Mr  Thomas  Shorte,  Phisition  in  Berry,  the  some  of  ffortye 
poundes.  Also  vnto  my  wife’s  nephewe  Mr  Robert  Bacon  five  pownds  Anuytie  out  of  my  Mannor 
of  Chedber.  R.  Drury.  Probatum  fuit  testamentum  suprascriptum  cum  Codicillo  annex  vicesimo 
septimo  die  Novembris,  1615,  Juramento  Domine  Anne  Drury,  Relicte,  &c.

Cozen  Henry  Drury  of  Stanninghall.  My  brother  Mr  Anthony  Drury  to  delyver  to  my  daughter  in  lawe  Rose  Claxton  the 
seale  Ringe  which  was  her  ffather's,  Mr  Lyster.  My  brother  Mr  Owen  Claxtou  &  my  sonne  Frauneis  Claxton.  My  verie  good 
Cozen  Mr  John  Gurden,  Esquire,  and  my  cozen  Amye  his  wife.  I  gyve  vnto  Roger  Drury  my  sonne  my  Mannor  of  Eccles 
in  the  countie  of  Norff.  and  my  messuage  in  Yarmouth.  My  messuages  &c.  in  Rashmere  and  Bradwell  co.  Stiff.  My  sonne  in 
lawe  Fraunces  Claxton  and  Rose  his  wife.  To  Drue  Drury  my  sonne  my  signett  of  golde  with  my  Armes,  the  gylt  cupp  which 
Sr  Drue  Drury  did  give  me  at  my  mariage,  and  all  the  plate  which  was  geven  him  at  his  Christeninge.  Vnto  Katherine  my 
wife  all  my  Mannors,  landes  &c.  in  Norff  and  Suff  duringe  her  life.  My  Mannors  of  Rollysby  and  Bills,  and  my  landes  in 
Bradwell  and  Gorleston.  I  doe  make  the  said  Katherine  my  sole  executor.  She  shall  gyve  good  and  sufficient  educacon  to  my 
two  sonnes  Drue  and  Roger,  first  at  Cambridge  then  at  the  Innes  of  Courte.  I  besech  Sr  Drue  Drury  the  he  will  give  me 
leave  to  appoynte  him  the  overseer  of  this  will.  And  I  gyve  him  one  Bason  and  Ewer  of  sylver  worth  twentie  poundes,  besides 
the  fashion  of  it.  A  Codicill  12th  June,  1599.  Katherine  my  wiffe  shall  sell  my  how.se  in  Yarmouth  called  the  Dolphins  which 
late  were  Thomas  Nesse  her  brother’s,  and  my  Coppeholde  lands  in  Smalborough  &  Dilham  and  my  tent’e  in  Yelverton.

The  Arms  of  Drury  of  Ireland  as  depicted  on  the  Funeral  Certificate  of  Katherine,

Bnto>  of  Clapton. 


Armorial  Hearings. 

The  arms  allowed  to  Francis  Drury  of  Swaffham  Prior  at  the  Cambridge  Visitation  in 
1619  were  Argent,  on  a  chief  Vert  a  cross  tan  between  two  mullets  Or  pierced  Gules,  an  annulet 
of  the  last  indicating  descent  from  a  fifth  son.  Such  a  fifth  son,  Thomas  Drury  of  Candellers  in 
Hessett  (see  pedigree,  p.  346),  brother  of  Sir  William  Drury  of  Rougham,  might  well  have  been 
the  great  grandfather  of  Thomas  Drury  of  Fincham,  the  more  immediate  ancestor  of  the 
Cambridgeshire  Drurys.  Other  Suffolk  Drurys,  as  is  well  known,  made  suggestive  wills  in  the 
fifteenth  and  sixteenth  centuries,  but  their  connection,  if  any,  with  the  Rougham  family  has 
not  as  yet  been  adequately  investigated. 

In  St.  George’s  Visitation  of  Cambridgeshire  and  Huntingdonshire,  1684  (College  of  Arms,  K.  7), 
there  is  a  tricking  of  the  shield  of  William  Drury  of  Earith  and  of  his  son  Richard  Drury, 
High  Sheriff  of  those  counties  in  1678.  It  agrees  substantially  with  that  described  above,  but 
the  mullets  are  not  pierced.  The  Crest,  a  greyhound,  Argent,  which  seems  to  be  leaping  rather 
than  running  and  is  not  collared  or  ringed,  is  charged  with  an  annulet,  Gules,  for  difference- 
On  the  Drury  tombstones  at  Claydon  the  Arms  have  the  chief  with  the  cross  tau  between 
the  mullets,  but  no  sign  of  cadency,  and  the  Crest  is  simply  a  greyhound  courant.

1  Charles  Suckling,  born  1578,  was  son  of  Robert  Suckling,  Esq.,  M.P.  for  Norwich,  by  his  third  wife,  Joan,  daughter  of 
William  Cardinall  of  Bromley  in  Essex,  and  widow  of  Robert  Vesey  of  Wix  Abbey,  who  died  1575.  (See  page  64,  Vesey  of  Wix 
Abbey.)  By  a  family  arrangement  he  succeeded  to  the  Woodton  estate,  on  his  father’s  death  in  1589.  He  was  a  Colonel  in 
the  Army,  and  purchased  the  Manor  of  Barsham  in  Suffolk  of  his  nephew,  Sir  John  Suckling,  Knt.,  the  Cavalier  Poet. 

Arms  : — Party,  per  pale,  Gules  and  Azure,  three  bucks,  trippant,  Or.

3 run»  of  legate. 


The  fall  of  the  house  of  Leziate  is  a  memorable  instance  of  the  vicissitudes  of  families. 
In  the  too  brief  memoir  ( Annual  Biography ,  Yol.  XIX)  of  Dr.  Joseph  Drury,  the  famous  Master 
of  Harrow,  himself  a  descendant  of  the  Leziate  family,  we  are  told  of  the  extravagance  of  its 

last  owner,  John  Drury,  who  lived  in  the  spendthrift  days  of  Charles  the  Second,  and  of  the 

sale  of  his  estates,  a  step  which  his  tried  friend,  Dr.  Gibson,  afterwards  Bishop  of  London, 
ineffectually  endeavoured  to  prevent.  In  the  Chancery  Proceedings  in  “  Drury  contra  Turner  ” 
( Beynardson ,  321/.,  68),  we  have  a  vivid  picture  of  the  ruined  gentleman,  who  had  entered  his 
pedigree  in  the  Norfolk  Visitation  not  many  years  before,  and  of  his  hopeless  endeavours  to  avert 
his  fate.  In  1680  he  took  the  fatal  step  of  borrowing  money.  In  1682  his  two  sons  became 
securities  for  the  payment  of  further  bonds.  In  1683  he  sold  his  broad  lands,  perhaps  provisionally, 
in  Leziate,  Ashwicken,  Holt,  East  Winch,  Middleton,  Mintling,  Bawsey,  Gayton  and  Glasthorpe. 

[Norfolk  Fines,  Hill,  35  and  36  Chas.  II.)  In  1684  he  tried  to  save  himself  by  a  second  marriage, 
but  the  lady’s  portion  was  smaller  than  he  had  expected.  ( Drury  c.  Hooke,  Reynardson,  82,  136.) 
In  1686  he  assigned  what  was  left  him  to  trustees.  And  then,  when  all  was  lost,  we  find  him 
ending  his  days  as  a  Warder  in  the  Tower.  William  Drury,  his  younger  son,  had  long  before  gone 
to  the  West  Indies,  where,  it  is  said,  he  became  a  buccaneer.  George  Drury,  his  eldest  son,  the 
sometime  heir  of  Leziate,  studied  law  at  Thavies’  Inn  in  1680,  and  at  the  Inner  Temple  in  1687,  but, 
pressed  by  debts,  absconded  to  Whitefriars,  the  “  Alsatia  ”  so  cleverly  depicted  in  the  “Fortunes 
of  Nigel.”  Marrying  a  second  and  richer  wife  in  1704,  George  Drury  was  sued  by  Sir  John 

Turner  of  King’s  Lynn,  his  father’s  ci’editor,  for  the  bond  he  had  countersigned  some  two  and 

twenty  years  before.  His  later  fortunes  are  not  so  clear.  He  made  his  will  as  George  Drury  of 

the  Inner  Temple,  gentleman,  in  1716,  and  it  was  proved  by  his  widow  in  January  1719,  old 
style.  One  of  his  grandsons,  Robert  Drury,  the  rollicking  dramatist,  whose  now  forgotten  plays 

repose  amongst  the  rarer  volumes  in  the  British  Museum,  died  young  ;  but  another,  Thomas 
Drury,  the  father  of  the  Head  Master  of  Harrow,  lived  to  an  advanced  age  and  retained  much 
traditional  knowledge  of  his  forefathers.  See  Life  of  Dr.  Joseph  Drury  in  the  “Annual  Biography 
and  Obituary,”  1835,  and  in  the  “Dictionary  of  National  Biography,”  Drury  of  Knightstone  in 
Burke’s  “Landed  Gentry,”  Vol.  Ill,  Supplement,  1849,  etc.,  etc. 

In  his  will,  dated  25th  Feb.  1716,  George  Drury,  of  the  Inner  Temple,  London,  Gentleman 
(being  then  about  sixty  years  of  age),  infirm  in  body  but  of  sound  mind,  bequeathed  a  guinea 
apiece  to  Robert  Drury,  his  son,  and  to  Eleanor,  his  daughter,  wife  of  William  Pitt.  The 

rest  of  his  estates  he  devised  to  Elizabeth,  his  wife,  and  to  her  heirs.  The  witnesses  were  Susan 
Bell,  John  Keighley,  and  James  Paget.  Probate  was  given  to  Elizabeth  Drury,  the  relict,  on 
the  22nd  day  of  January  1719.

Apart  from  Fines  and  Subsidy  Rolls,  there  are  but  few  evidences  relating  to  the  earlier 
Langhams  of  Suffolk  in  our  public  offices  of  record.  These,  however,  abundantly  testify  that  they 
were  knights  and  gentlemen,  and  that  they  held  the  manor  of  Langham  Hall  for  many  generations. 
The  inscriptions  to  their  memory,  formerly  on  the  floor  of  Langham  church,  have  long  since 
disappeared,  but  their  arms  (Argent,  a  fess,  Gules,  aud  a  label  of  three  points,  Azure)  still 
remained  on  four  of  the  faces  of  the  octagonal  font  when  Davy  visited  the  place  in  1843.  An 
excellent  account  of  their  alliances  and  descents  was  printed  by  Morant  in  his  “  History  of  Essex.” 
They  resided  much  in  this  latter  county  after  the  marriage,  circa  1341,  of  Sir  William  de  Langham 
with  the  sister  and  heiress  of  Sir  John  de  Wateville,  who  brought  with  her  the  manors  of  Panfield 
and  Hempsted.  These,  together  with  their  old  patrimony  of  Langham  in  Suffolk,  ultimately  passed, 
by  the  marriage  of  Alice  Langham,  the  heiress  of  the  family,  to  the  Cottons.  The  fullest  pedigree 
of  the  Langhams  of  Langham  is  that  compiled  by  Sampson  Lennard  early  in  the  seventeenth 
century  (Harl.  MS.  1500).  It  is  given,  in  italics ,  with  additions  from  other  sources  (including 
Harl.  MS.  1137),  on  the  next  page.

Armorial  Scarings,  rtr. 

There  were  Laughams  of  Mildenhall  and  Bury  St.  Edmunds  in  the  fifteenth  and  sixteenth 
centuries.  Simon  Langham,  of  the  latter  place,  was  one  of  the  sons-in-law  of  William  Payton  of 
Risby,  whose  will  was  proved  in  1556,  and  one  of  the  plaintiffs  in  Payton  contra  Hammond  in 
1588.  See  Pedigree  of  Payton,  Hammond  and  Langham  of  London,  on  page  262.  Another  som 
in-law  was  Thomas  Bright,  whose  descendants  entered  pedigrees  in  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1664. 
“  The  Brights  of  Suffolk,  England,”  printed  at  Boston,  Massachusetts,  one  of  the  best  family 
histories  extant,  contains  many  allusions  to  their  Langham  cousins,  and  reproduces  a  letter  from 
George  Langham,  afterwards  of  Clapham  in  Surrey,  to  Thomas  Bright  of  Netherhall  near  Bury, 
dated  22  May  1651.  It  relates  to  Thomas  Bright’s  son,  then  in  Malaga,  where  the  Langhams 
had  a  factor,  and  alludes  to  the  writer’s  late  uncle  Scales,  his  brother  Harvey  and  his  cousin, 
Joseph  Withers.  It  will  be  seen  from  his  will,  which  we  subjoin,  that  George  Langham,  son  of 
Simon  Langham  and  Rose  Payton,  and  who  is  described  in  his  pedigree  as  one  of  the  Captains 
of  the  City  of  London,  was  engaged  officially  in  the  Civil  Wars,  and  contemplating  the  possibility 
of  death  in  the  service.  This  was  in  1643.  In  1631  the  Arms  of  the  Langhams  of  Langham, 
his  knightly  predecessors  in  the  days  of  the  Plantagenets,  Argent,  a  fess  Gules,  a  label  of  three 
points,  Azure,  had  been  allowed  him  by  the  heralds,  when  he  entered  his  pedigree  in  the  Visitation 
of  London.  The  same  arms  were  confirmed  to  George  Langham,  his  son,  the  correspondent  of  Thomas 
Bright,  at  the  Visitation  of  Surrey  in  1662. 


Will  of  Qknrge  Utangbam,  1643. 

I,  George  Langham  of  London,  Marchantailor.  considering  the  certainty  of  death,  and  more 
espially  calling  to  mind  the  employment  wch  it  hath  pleased  god  at  this  tyme  to  call  me  vnto, 
and  the  danger  therof,  do  make  this  my  last  will.  In  the  first  place  I  bequeath  my  sowle  vnto 

god  my  maker  and  to  Jesus  Christ  my  redemer,  and  my  body  to  the  earth  where  it  shall 

please  god  to  suffer  it  to  be  layd.  My  psonal  estate  being  much  dimminished  by  the  will  of 

god,  my  will  is  that  yt  be  devided  into  five  equall  partes  :  of  which  I  doe  bequeath  fower  to  my 
fower  children  wch  are  not  as  yet  advanced  in  porcon  ;  that  is  to  say,  my  sonnes  Henry  Langham> 
Thomas  Langham,  William  Langham,  and  my  daughter  Elizabeth  Langham,  and  the  other  fyft  part 
I  doe  leave  to  executor  to  pforme  legacies.  I  desire  my  executo1'  to  remember  my  sister  Porter 
so  long  as  she  liveth.  Vnto  my  two  granchildren  Jon  Juxson,  eldest  sonne  to  my  son  in-law  Mr 
John  Juxson  of  Morclacke,  and  vnto  George  Harvie,  eldest  sonne  vnto  my  daughter  Harvie,  ten 
poundes  a  peece  at  their  ages  of  twenty  one  yeares.  And  yf  it  shall  please  god  that  I  dye  in 

this  Service,  my  will  is  that  the  horse  wch  I  borrowed  of  my  good  frend,  Mr  Edward  Crople  of 

London,  mercer,  be  restored  vnto  him,  or  the  value  of  him  if  he  be  left  in  the  service,  and 

a  tierse  of  Clarret  wine  be  given  him  for  his  love  and  courtesie  in  lending  me  that  horse.  Vnto 

the  poore  of  Garlicke  Hive  five  pounds.  Vnto  the  Company  of  Merchant  tailors.  I  doe  ordaine 
my  eldest  sonne,  George  Langham,  sole  executor,  yf  he  be  liveing  after  my  deeease.  And  yf 
it  shall  please  God  to  call  him  out  of  this  mortall  life  before  me,  I  will  my  second  sonne,  Henry

It  would  appear  from  the  will  of  John  Langham  in  the  Bury  Register,  dated  1476,  that  the  Langhams  of 
Bury  St.  Edmunds  and  of  Mildenhall  were  very  nearly  related.  As  late  as  the  beginning  of  the  present  century 
there  were  still  Langhams  at  Mildenhall,  one  of  whom,  William  Langham,  had  an  only  surviving  son,  John  Langham 
of  Northwold  (born  3  May  1795,  and  died  16  Oct.  1847),  who  assumed,  by  Royal  license  in  1813,  the  arms  and 
surname  of  Carter,  in  lieu  of  his  patronymic,  and  was  a  J.P.  and  D.L.  for  Norfolk.  He  married,  9  Jan.  1819, 
Mary  Anne,  daughter  of  William  George  Daniel  Tyssen  of  Fouldon  Hall,  and  has  left  numerous  descendants.

Robert  Jettor  of  Lowestoft,  testator’s  grandson,  entered  his  pedigree  in  the  Suffolk  Visitation 
of  1612.  William  Bishop  of  Yarmouth,  the  son-in-law,  entered  his.  at  a  much  earlier  date,  in  the 
Visitation  of  Norfolk.  Like  the  Bedingfields  and  the  Rokewodes,  the  Jettors  were  distinguished 
Roman  Catholics,  and  were  fined  for  Recusancy  in  the  days  of  Queen  Elizabeth  and  King  James.

Will  of  Slijateb  JUttolb,  1788. 

Being  in  sound  memory  and  having  an  absolute  right  to  give  my  fortune  to  who  I  please, 

I  Elizabeth  Arnold  of  Stratford  le  Bow  in  the  Co.  of  Essex  do  make  my  last  Will  &  Testament 

as  follows. 

I  give  to  my  daughter  Caroline  Allen  my  estates  in  North  Cove  and  Lowestoft,  and  my 
estate  in  Stratford  left  me  by  my  cousin  Mr  Sontley  South,  also  in  the  three  pr  cent.  Bank  Consul 
Annuities,  in  reduced  annuities,  in  South  Sea  Stock,  in  new  and  old  annuities  and  Exchequer  Orders, 
and  stock  in  the  funds,  in  Trust  to  my  Grandson  and  Grand  daughter  Hatch,  Mr  John  Addington 
in  the  Temple,  Mr  John  James  of  Worton,  to  be  paid  to  my  said  daughter  for  her  natural  life,  and 

at  her  decease  to  go  to  my  Grandson  &  Grand  daughter  Hatch  for  ever. 

Item.  All  my  Bank  Stock  to  my  Grand  daughter  Wilmina  Caroline  Hatch  to  her  sole  use 
for  life,  and  at  her  decease  [to  be]  equally  divided  between  her  children. 

Item.  To  my  grand  daughter  Caroline  Elizabeth  Hatch  two  thousand  pounds,  to  be  laid 
out  to  accumulate  untill  she  arrives  at  the  age  of  21  years. 

Item  in  legacies  I  give  as  follows : — To  Admiral  John  Carter  Allen  one  thousand  pounds. 
To  my  Grandson  and  Grand  daughter  Hatch  five  hundred  pounds  each  To  my  nephew  John  South 
Morse  £500.  To  Mr  John  Addington  in  the  Temple  £500.  To  Mr  John  James  of  Worton  £500. 
To  Mr  Aldous  Arnold  senior  of  Lowestoft  merch*  £300.  To  Mr  John  Fowler  of  N.  Yarmouth  £300. 
To  Mr  George  Bristowe  of  MercU  Taylors  Hall  £100.  To  Mr  Talbot  of  Stratford  £100,  &c.  &c. 
As  I  have  changed  my  intention  being  buried  at  Lowestoft  I  now  [wish]  to  be  buried  at  Little 
Ilford  in  a  vault  prepared  for  me,  in  linen,  in  a  Leaden  Coffin  and  in  another  covered  with  black 
cloth,  black  nails  and  Copper  Plate  on  the  lid  with  my  name ;  no  hatchment  to  be  put  out  nor 
rooms  hung  in  black,  but  to  be  buried  as  privately  as  decency  will  permit.  I  nominate  and  appoint 
my  Grandson  and  Grand  daughter  Hatch  &  Mr  John  Addington  of  the  Temple  my  executors,  and 
do  declare  this  to  be  my  last  will  where  unto  I  have  this  day  of  May,  18th,  1788  set  my  hand 
&  seal.  Elizabeth  Arnold.  In  the  presence  at  my  request  of  my  undermentioned  three  friends. 
Jno  Snelgrave,  Edward  Parsons,  Josiah  Price.

The  Arms  of  Richard  Aldous,  as  depicted  on  his  monument  in  Huntingfield  Church,  are  a  lion  rampant  holding  a  ring 
in  his  dexter  paw.  Crest  :  Out  of  a  Viscount’s  Coronet,  a  demi-lion  rampt.  ;  in  his  sinister  paw  a  sword  erect. 

Those  claimed  by  John  Aldous  of  Moulton,  at  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  1664.  who  was  probably  one  of  the  same  family, 

were  Argent,  a  chevron  between  three  birds  displaying  rising  Gules ;  on  a  chief  Sable,  three  mullets  of  the  field.  The  crest 
was  a  bird  rising  Gules.  Harl.  MS.  10S5. 

The  constant  intercourse  between  our  sea  coast  towns  in  the  sixteenth  and  seventeenth  centuries,  a  fact  scarcely  sufficiently 
realized  at  the  present  time,  lends  some  support  to  the  assumption  that  the  Arnolds  of  Lowestoft,  Dunwich  and  Cromer  ( Norf. 
Visitns.  Harl.  Soc.),  all  belonged  to  the  same  stock.  That  some  of  the  latter  did  settle  in  Suffolk  is  known  from  the  Will 

of  Gertrude  Arnold  of  Oxnead,  1624,  and  from  the  pedigree  of  John  Arnold,  of  Battisford,  in  the  Suffolk  Visitation  of  Sir 

Edward  Bysshe.  These  Battsford  Arnolds  bore  for  their  Arms,  Sable,  a  chevron  between  three  dolphins  embowed  Argent. 
Their  Crest  was,  On  a  wreath  a  dolphin  embowed  Argent.  Harl.  MS.  10S5.

Corrigenda  et  Addenda. 


Page  25.  Winthrop  of  Groton.  Alice  “  Henny,”  1st  wife  of  Adam  Winthrop.  Probably  Alice  Hunne.  See  the  Cely- 
Hunne-Byrd  matter  on  pp.  166  and  223.  By  a  typographical  mistake  she  is  stated  to  have  died  25  June 
1533.  The  month  should  be  January.  See  the  Latin  pedigree  of  Winthrop,  p.  4. 

Ibid.  William  Winthrop  is  here  stated  to  have  died  2  March  1682,  but  the  Latin  pedigree  (p.  6)  gives  the 
date  1  March  1581,  which  is  probably  correct. 

Ibid.  Jane  Winthrop,  who  married  Thomas  Gostlin,  is  said  to  have  been  married  on  Jan.  3,  1612.  This  is  a 
printer’s  error.  The  date  ( see  p.  6)  was  Jan.  6.  She  did  not  die,  as  here  stated,  in  1616,  but  was 

living  as  late  as  15  Feb.  1663,  when  she  is  mentioned  in  her  sister  Downing’s  letter.  See  p.  95. 

Page  26.  Winthrop  of  Boston.  By  a  typographical  error  Deane  Winthrop  is  described  as  having  been  born  in  1632. 
This  should  be  1623. 

Ibid.  John  Winthrop  (last  descent  but  one)  did  not  die,  1819,  at  Baton  Rouge,  but  at  Washington,  U.S. 

Pages  26-27.  John  Winthrop,  eldest  son  of  John  Winthrop  and  Mary  Forth,  was  reallyT  born  12  Feb.  1605,  Old 
Style,  as  stated  on  p.  7.  But  on  pp.  26-27,  the  New  Style  date,  1606  is  given.  Feb.  12  is  transformed, 
‘by  typographical  error,  into  Feb.  15. 

Page  26.  John  Winthrop  was  undoubtedly  married  to  Mary  Forth  on  the  16th  of  April  1605,  as  stated  on  p.  7  ; 
but  the  month  is  here  erroneously  given  as  March. 

Page  27.  Winthrop  of  New  London.  Martha  Fones,  first  wife  of  John  Winthrop,  jun.,  was  married  in  February, 
1631,  New  Style,  not  1630  a3  stated  in  the  text. 

Ibid.  Fitz  John  Winthrop,  it  turns  out,  was  born  in  Boston,  not  in  “  Ipswich,”  as  often  stated. 

Page  28.  Winthrop  of  Antigua.  The  first  volume  of  Mr.  Vere  Langford  Oliver’s  admirable  History  of  Antigua  had  not 

been  issued  when  our  account  of  the  Winthrops  of  that  island  went  to  the  press.  He  points  out  that 
Sarah  Winthrop,  wife  of  Colonel  Samuel  Jones,  was  not  “  probably  s.p.,”  as  is  usually  represented,  but 
that  she  married  2d  Colonel  Edward  Byam,  brother  of  her  sister’s  husband,  and  left  issue  by  him. 

Page  30.  Winthrop  of  London.  The  Rev.  Edward  Winthrop,  who  died  in  1824  (not  1826),  was  Vicar  of  Dareuth, 

co.  Kent,  and  not  Rector  of  West  Mailing,  as  to  which  we  were  misinformed.  His  wife  was  daughter 

of  Henry  Everleigh,  gent.,  of  Teignton,  co.  Devon.  His  daughter  Martha  died  unmarried  in  1855,  but  her 
sister  Frances  married  in  1845  the  Rev.  John  Woodruff,  Vicar  of  Upchurch,  Kent,  and  left  issue,  inter 
al.  the  Rev.  Charles  Everleigh  Woodruff,  M.A.  of  Oriel  College,  Oxford,  and  now  Rector  of  Otterden. 

Ibid.  William  Winthrop,  sometime  Fellow  of  St.  John’s  College,  Cambridge,  married  Frances  Mary,  daughter  of 
the  Rev.  George  Feacliam,  Vicar  of  Dorking,  Surrey. 

Page  41.  Sharpe  of  Islington.  “John  Bullen  ”  should  be  John  Buller.  This  was,  perhaps,  the  “cosen  Bulwer” 
who  came  to  Adam  Winthrop’s  house  a  day  or  two  before  he  went  to  see  his  cousin  Joan  Muskett, 
2  June  1597.  Adam  Winthrop’s  Diary. 

Page  65.  Alabaster  of  Hadleigh.  According  to  the  parish  registers  of  St.  Peter’s,  Cornhill,  Thomas  Alabaster 

described  in  Adam  Winthrop’s  Diary  as  having  died  in  1620,  was  buried  June  4th  1624.  It  is  not 

always  easy  to  explain  the  conflicting  dates  of  contemporary  documents.  In  this  instance  it  is  not 
improbable  that  different  persons  were  referred  to. 

Page  64.  Vesey  of  Wix.  Joan,  daughter  of  William  Cardinall  of  Bromley,  and  widow  of  Robert  Vesey  of  Wix, 
married  secondly  Robert  Suckling,  Esq.,  M.P.  for  Norwich,  19  Nov.  1577.  Her  son  Charles  Suckling  of 
Woodton,  Norfolk  and  Barsham,  Suffolk,  intermarried  with  the  Drurys  of  Aylsham  and  of  Besthorpe. 
See  pp.  370  and  355. 

Page  76.  Still  of  Hadleigh.  For  the  will  of  George  Still,  B.D.,  the  Bishop’s  brother,  see  p.  165. 

Page  86.  Fones  of  Nustbed.  On  the  last  line  of  the  ancient  pedigree  of  his  family  Samuel  Fones  is  described 

as  “act.  12  a0  1628.”  In  the  modern  pedigree  which  follows  he  is  said  to  be  “aged  11  a0  1629.” 

The  latter  date  is  given  in  the  Inquisition  of  his  father,  Thomas  Fones.  Discrepancies  of  this  kind  are 
not  uncommon  in  old  documents,  which  were  based  oftentimes  upon  verbal  evidence  only7.
