Page  87.  Subsequent  discoveries,  including  the  will  of  Marj’  Paul,  given  on  p.  168,  and  those  of  her  sister  Sarah 
Fones  (P.C.C.  46  Edmunds),  and  her  cousin,  Eleazar  Hasell  (P.C.C.  8  Isham),  have  established  an 
important  modification  of  the  pedigree  of  Fones  of  Suffolk.  Mary,  the  daughter  of  Eleazar  Dunkon, 
was  the  wife  of  Dr.  Thomas  Fones,  and  not,  as  here  erroneously  stated,  of  Samuel  Fones,  his  father. 
In  this  instance,  as  sometimes  happens,  the  lives  of  father  and  son,  were  almost  contemporaneous,  and 
each  had  a  wife  named  Mary.  Barnaby  and  Anne  Fones  were  devisees,  not  of  Eleazar  Dunkon,  but  of 
their  brother,  the  Doctor,  who  pre  deceased  his  father  by  fifteen  years. 

Page  99.  Downing  of  Ipswich.  Susan  Downing,  wife  of  Francis  Kirby,  had  previously  married  Joseph  Carter,  by 
whom  she  left  issue.  See  the  will  of  Richard  Blades,  1634,  in  the  Commissary  Court  of  London. 

Page  118.  Fokth  Pedigree,  Candler  MSS.  “His  wife  had  a  child,  but  he  disowned  it.’’  The  story  of  the  domestic 

disagreements  of  Charles  Forth  and  Elizabeth  Jernegau,  his  wife,  is  given  in  a  suit  in  the  Court  of 
Requests,  Hunt’s  Series,  27,  45.  Two  children  were  born  of  the  marriage,  but  the  husband  is  described 
as  a  spendthrift  and  a  rover,  and  the  Blois  MS.  tells  us  that  he  was  ultimately  disinherited  by  his 
father. 

Page  119.  Forth  of  Hadleigh.  The  parish  register  of  St.  Dionis  Backchurch,  London,  shows  that  William  Forth 
married  Elizabeth  Powell  17  Jan.  1540,  Old  Style. 

Ibid.  William  Forth  of  Hadleigh,  who  died  in  1599,  had  but  one  wife,  Dorothy  Harvey,  as  shown  on  p.  315. 

Joan  Kene,  described  in  the  MSS.  as  his  second  wife,  was  in  reality  Dorothy  Harvey’s  mother. 

Page  144.  Clopton  of  Groton.  The  excellent  pedigree  of  Clopton  in  Add.  MS.  5523,  tells  us  (fo.  84b)  that  “  Will’m 

Clopton,  now  of  Groton  in  com  Suff.  (the  father  of  Thomasine  Winthrop)  was  y  1  y  builded  and 

dwelte  at  Castlelynes  in  p’ish  of  Groton  p’d,  who  haueinge  spent  all  his  fath’s  lands  and  patrimonye,  he  became 
heire  to  his  Yncle  frauncz  of  Melford  p'ke.  This  Wm  Clopton  now  is  an  Esq  vizt’  one  of  if  Justices  for 
y ‘  Hundred  of  Babrega  1614.” 

Page  145.  Clopton  of  Liston.  The  pedigree  of  Clopton  of  Liston,  Add.  MS.  5523,  fo.  85a,  written  in  1713,  adds  so 
much  to  the  knowledge  of  the  later  descents  of  that  family,  that  we  insert  it  in  this  place.

Goodwin  of  Bull’s  Hall.  Two  seventeenth  century  pedigrees,  the  one  in  the  College  of  Arms  and 
the  other  in  the  Free  Library  at  Norwich,  throw  much  light  upon  the  marriages  and  descendants  of 
Cecily  Reedham.  The  first,  dated  about  1633,  gives  the  common  ancestry  of  Sir  Thurston  Smith  of 
Cratfield  in  Suffolk  and  Sir  Owen  Symth  of  Ermingland  in  Norfolk,  and  the  second,  copied  in  1657, 
relates  to  the  Spelmans.  Thomas  Spelman  of  Norwich,  it  tells  us,  third  sou  of  Erasmus  Spelman  of 
Beeston,  near  Litcham,  in  Norfolk,  married  Cecily,  daughter  and  heir  of  Reedham,  widow  of  Raphe 
Goodwyn  of  Ipswich,  and,  before  that,  of  Smyth  of  Suffolk.  From  these  and  other  sources  the  following 
brief  pedigree  may  be  deducted  : —

Goodwin  of  Torrington.  John  Ingold  (not  Inglose)  of  Kesgrave,  in  Suffolk,  by  his  will,  Arch.  Suffolc, 
8  July  1535,  devised  lands  in  Little  Bealings,  etc.,  to  Henry  Goodwiu  and  his  children.  By  a  printer’s 
error  the  date  is  twice  given  as  1635. 

Hammond  of  Ufford.  Thomas  Hammond,  who  emigrated  to  Norway,  was  known  there  as  “Thomas 
Englishman.”  He  came  to  Troudhjem  in  the  reign  of  Charles  II,  and  has  left  many  descendants.  His 
grandson,  Thomas  Angell,  who  was  very  wealthy,  fouuded  the  famous  charity  called  by  his  name, 
providing  especially  for  such  of  his  kindred  as  might  fall  into  poverty  in  future  years. 

Gordon  of  Letton.  Abigail  Kuyvett,  who  married  Martin  Sedley,  was  daughter  of  John  Knyvett  and 
sister  of  Sir  Thomas.  Sir  Richard  Saltonstall  should  be  styled  “of  Yorkshire.”  Sir  Richard  Saltonstall 
of  Essex  was  quite  another  man,  but  the  two  are  frequently  confounded.  A  number  of  letters  from 
Brampton  Gurdon  to  John  Wintlirop,  Governor  of  Massachusetts,  are  to  be  found  in  the  Fourth  Series 
of  the  Massachusetts  Historical  Society’s  Collections.  John  Gurdon  was  M.P.  for  Ipswich,  1640. 

Burrouqh  of  Wickhambrook.  In  the  light  of  nineteenth  century  criticism,  Cotton  Mather’s  action  at 
the  trial  and  execution  of  George  Burrough  is  only  to  be  excused  on  the  ground  of  intense  and 
inherited  prejudice.  But  to  speak  of  him,  generally,  as  a  “fanatical  divine”  is  to  do  him  less  than 
justice.  To  no  writer  are  Anglo-American  genealogists  more  indebted  for  the  links  which  bind  the  New 
England  emigrants  to  their  kinsmen  of  the  old  world  than  to  the  gossiping,  learned  and  enthusiastic 
author  of  Magnalia  Christi  Americana. 

For  “.  .  .  entered  Harvard  College  1870,”  in  the  accouut  of  George  Burrough  of  New  England,  substitute 
“ A.B.  Harvard  College  1670.”  Although  described  as  “clerk”  in  his  indictment,  there  is  no  record  of 
his  ordination.  He  was,  doubtless,  a  Nonconformist  minister.

Appleton  of  Waldingfikld.  The  inscriptions  are  in  Little  Waldingfield  church,  not  at  Great  Waldingfield, 
as  stated  by  Weever. 

Ibid.  John  Appleton  was  second ,  not  third,  in  descent  from  John  Appleton  of  Waldingfield  Parva,  who 
died  14  H.  4. 

It  is  but  right  to  say  that  the  earlier  descents  of  Appleton,  as  given  in  Harl.  MSS.  1198,  1560,  etc.,  have 
never  before  been  criticised  ;  nor,  indeed,  with  the  exception  of  details  pointed  out  in  the  footnote, 
have  they  ever  been  disproved.  The  question,  here  perhaps  unnecessarily  raised,  as  to  the  exact 
paternity  of  William  Appleton,  the  husband  of  Rose  Sexton,  would  never  have  occurred  had  the  usual 
Inquisitions,  Fines,  etc.,  connected  with  the  inheritance  of  feudal  estates,  been  extant  in  his  case. 

Dkury  of  Sussex.  Alice,  widow  of  John  Drury,  LL.D.,  married  Francis  Nevill,  Esq.,  2  Oct.  1616,  and 
made  her  will  14  Oct.  1618.  Chat  1  B.  A.  D.D.  44,  49,  Drury  c.  Jordan.  Her  grandson,  Francis 
Drury,  was  of  Watergate  in  1664,  and  his  wife  was  daughter  of  John  Weston,  Esq.,  of  Speldhurst,  co- 
Kent.  Chas  I.  B.  X  A.  D.D.  13,  45  Drury  c.  Horton. 

Drury  of  Hawstkad.  Henry  Drury  of  Ickworth  was  Sheriff  of  Norfolk  and  Suffolk  1423-30,  and  M.P 
for  Suffolk  1433  and  1435. 

Drury  of  Besthorpe.  Catherine,  eldest  daughter  of  William  Drury  the  first  of  Besthorpe,  is  called 
Catherine,  not  Mary,  in  her  grandfather’s  will.  Catherine,  wife  of  Nicholas  Drury  of  Intwood  1691, 
was  daughter  of  Sir  Robert  Jenney,  not  Sir  John.  Jermyn  and  Norris  quoted  by  Davy  in  his  MSS. 
Drury  of  Hedgerley.  William  Drury,  the  heir  of  Hedgerley,  was  still  engaged  with  his  case  against 
Darell  in  December  1645,  being  then  blind  and  weak,  with  only  an  annuity  of  £40  a  year.  Calendar 
of  House  of  Lords  MSS.  in  the  sixth  Report  of  the  Historical  MSS.  Commission.  Frances,  his  sister, 
married,  1633,  Henry  Allen,  Esq.,  of  the  Inner  Temple.  License  in  Faculty  Office.  Harl.  Soc.  Vol.  24. 
Rowland  Hynde  was  of  Hedsor  (not  Hedsworth),  co.  Bucks.  He  died  in  1608,  and  Elizabeth,  his  wife, 
11  Jany.  1606.  There  is  a  brass  to  their  memory  in  Hedsor  church.  There  is  also  a  brass  in  Penn 

church  to  Dame  Susan  Drury,  who  died  3  Feb.  1640,  and  her  daughter  Sarah,  wife  of  John  Penn. 
Lipscomb’s  Buckinghamshire.  Anne,  sister  of  Sir  Henry  Drury,  married,  9  July  1605,  Austin  Alexander. 
Hedgerley  Parish  Register. 

Arnold  of  Lowestoft.  Will  of  Aldous  Charles  Arnold,  fifth  line,  for  “Wringfield”  read  Wingfield. 

Ibid.  There  is  a  fine  monument  in  St.  Margaret’s  church,  Lowestoft,  over  the  north  door,  to  the  memory 
of  Aldous  Arnold  and  his  three  wives,  surmounted  by  the  aims,  Sable,  a  chevron  Argent,  between 
three  dolphins  embowed  of  the  same.  Crest,  a  dolphin  embowed  Argent. 

There  is  a  monument  in  St.  Mary’s  Church,  Bungay,  “  To  the  memory  of  Peregrey  Browne,  gent.,  who 
died  Jan.  2nd  1767,  aged  77  years;  and  of  Elizabeth  his  wife  who  died  June  4th  1773,  aged  77  years.” 
The  Arms  are  Argent,  on  a  beud  Azure  (or  Sable  ?)  three  eagles  displayed  Or.

-Winthrop  of  London.  For  “  Everleigh,"  read  Eyeleigh.” 

Fonks  of  Nusteed.  Samuel  Fones  the  younger  is  incidentally  named  in  the  will  of  his  father,  Samuel 

Fones,  in  1693,  not  in  that  of  his  brother,  Thomas  Fones.  It  is  probable  that  he  was  then  dead. 

Downing  of  Ipswich.  James  Downing  went  to  New  England  in  1630,  not  1640,  as  stated  in  the  text. 

Winthrop  of  Groton.  The  first  wife  of  Adam  Winthrop  died  in  1533,  not  1538,  as  here  erroneously 
printed. 

Drury  of  Besthorpe.  There  is,  apparently,  some  confusion  in  the  early  descents  of  this  family  as  given 

in  the  MSS.  It  is  stated  in  the  Inquisition  post  mortem  of  Charles  Drury,  taken  35th  Henry  VIII, 

that  long  before  his  death  one  Robert  Drury  Esqr  was  seized  of  a  Manor  in  Besthorpe,  which  he 

enfeoffed  to  one  Robert  Drury  of  Besthorpe  and  Ela  his  wife,  with  remainder  to  Charles  Drury  their 
son  and  heir.  Robert  Drury  of  Besthorpe  had  died,  but  Ela  was  still  living.  Charles  Drury  their 
son  deceased  23d  Feb.  32d  Henry  VIII,  William  Drury  his  son  and  heir  being  of  the  age  of  four 
years  and  upwards. 

Drury  of  Leziate.  On  the  19th  of  March,  1692,  the  Administration  of  Elizabeth  Drury,  late  of  St.  Giles’, 
Cripplegate,  widow,  was  granted  to  John  Jurin,  the  guardian  of  Isaac  Drury,  a  minor,  her  natural  and 
lawful  son.  Admans.  P.C.C. 

Arnold  of  Lowestoft. — Frances  Arnold  was  daughter  and  heir  of  Peregrey  Browne.  For  Birchinshaw  (see 
about  the  middle  of  the  pedigree)  read  Byrchinshaw. 

Edward  Arnold  was  Bailiff  of  Dunwicli  in  1314  and  1325.  In  1334  (7  Edw.  Ill)  the  feefarm  rent  of 
sixteen  pence  was  due  to  the  King  “  de  heredibus  Edmundi  Arnold  pro  Christepenysaker.”  Sir  Henry 
Harnold,  “Knight  and  Freer,”  was  buried  in  the  Black  Friar’s  church  there.  ( Weever.  p.  720).  In  1496 
Ameys  Arnold  “  gaff  nets  to  the  Cherche,  viii3  vid.”  See  Gardner’s  History  of  Dunwich.
